speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. Mr. Speaker, it is true that the Minister of Supply and Services has been asked to assist the Secretary of State for External Affairs in an advisory capacity, and I think that is a good idea in view of the increasing importance of our relations with Francophone countries. speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: REASON FOR CHANGE FROM EXCURSION FARE PLAN TO CHARTER CLASS FARES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am quite aware of the reasons for the change. It was intentionally designed to ensure that passengers, where possible, were attracted to seats which otherwise would be empty, and the lower priced fares were to be used in order to attract them there. It is obviously in the over-all interest of the Canadian flying public to have as many seats filled as possible in order that the cost of flying be shared as widely as possible. The excursion fares did not serve this purpose as well since they simply added additional pressure to the seats available in a limited way at peak periods. Charter class fares do the other thing, which is attract passengers to the non-peak periods and in that way attempt to raise the over-all load factor, which is something I am interested in seeing achieved.

Would the minister not agree that reverting to the new charter class fare structure was designed around the preknowledge that it would restrict the number of seats that are available, thus rendering to the Canadian flying public a number of seats that is totally unacceptable to the vast majority of Canadians who want to travel by air. Does the minister not agree that that was done deliberately? As the minister well knows, and based on inquiries I made today, it is not a question of not being able to get a seat before Labour day, you cannot get one until well after the new year.

Order, please. Yesterday, by way of a question of privilege, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar drew attention to some words used by the Prime Minister during the question period. According to our precedents, the use of unparliamentary language has always been a matter of order. The use of unparliamentary language is disorder and it is quite properly brought to the attention of the Chair by way of a point of order. It is true that it is often raised by way of a question of privilege also, and though this is an inaccurate practice it is certainly not an unpopular one and there is nothing extraordinary about the hon. member having raised this matter by way of a question of privilege. When it occurs, however, it is disorder and it is, therefore, more correctly raised by way of a point of order.
Equally clearly, in accordance with our practice, after the matter is brought to the attention of the Chair an interval usually follows and the member who is accused of having used impolite language, or intemperate language or, in broader terms, unparliamentary language, is usually given an opportunity to withdraw such an expression and indicate that it was not intended to be used in an offensive way. The matter having been raised, last evening, just after the taking of the vote, the Prime Minister rose in his place and indicated that the language attributed to him was, indeed, the language he used. He told the House he did not intend to offend, and he withdrew the remark. In these circumstances, it does not constitute, within our practice, a question of privilege which ought to be put to the House in an appropriate way. However, it does constitute a valid point of order for the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar to have raised. Equally, it has been disposed of by virtue of the withdrawal of the remark by the Prime Minister at about a quarter to seven last evening.

Sometimes the choice for the Chair, in having to decide whether or not particular language is unparliamentary, is invidious. When a member comes forward and says, regardless of whether the language used falls within the category of correct etiquette or lack of it, or impoliteness, that he wishes to withdraw it, the Chair is relieved of the burden of having to make a decision.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION SUBSIDIES
speechtext: Did the government conduct any studies in the past five years comparing the relative subsidization of the various modes of transportation and, if so, in each case (a) by whom (b) on what date was it (i) commenced (ii) completed (c) has it been publicly released and, if not, for what reason (d) are copies of the study available and, if so, from whom?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION SUBSIDIES
speechtext:
In so far as Transport Canada is concerned: two studies have been conducted in the period 1970-75 regarding the annual costs and revenues of transportation in Canada by modes and the relative subsidization of each mode.
1)	(a) The first series of studies were undertaken by the Canadian Transport Commission, dealing with the air, marine, road and rail modes and covered the period 1955-1969. (b)(i) The studies were commenced in the fall of 1970 and (ii) completed by approximately the following dates; Air, Fall. 1972; Marine, February 1973; Road, Fall 1972; Rail, April 1973. (c) All the studies except the one on rail were publicly released through Information Canada, (d) These are available through the Department of Supply and Services; the rail study is also available through the Research Branch of the CTC.
2)	(a) As part of the Transportation Task Force's policy review, an update of the CTC studies was undertaken by the CTC. (b)(i) It commenced in January 1975 and (ii) Was completed in May 1975. It covered the period from 1969-1973.
(c)	Copies of the report were made available in summary form originally through Transport Canada and later the Department of Supply and Services, (d) These documents are available through the Department of Supply and Services.
In so far as the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs is concerned: studies within the sphere of responsibility of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs relate to the urban component of the overall transportation sector. The ministry is conducting several internal policy studies which analyse costs and subsidies required for urban transportation. One study, conducted by the Transportation Development Agency and the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs on the total cost of urban travel commenced in the fall of 1975 and was completed in the spring of 1976. Current plans call for this study to be released publicly later this year when the latest cost/subsidy information has been incorporated.

speechtext:
that Bill C-50, to amend the Judges Act and other acts in respect of judicial matters, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, one of the great responsibilities of the Minister of Justice and all members of the House is to ensure that the judiciary of this country is maintained in a position where it can continue to carry out effectively, intelligently and independently the heavy duties that rest upon our judges. It is with this sense of responsibility that I have brought before this House the measures contained in Bill C-50 and move the adoption of that bill. Before turning to some of the specific provisions contained in the bill, it is perhaps useful to remind ourselves of the role and status of the judiciary in our system of government. Sir William Holdsworth put it well when he said:
The judges hold an office to which is annexed the function of guarding the supremacy of the law. It is because they are holders of an office to which the guardianship of this fundamental constitutional principle is entrusted, that the judiciary forms one of the three great divisions into which the power of the state is divided. The judiciary has separate and autonomous powers just as truly as the king or parliament.
While Sir William was obviously speaking of the British judiciary in the United Kingdom, his remarks are equally apt to describe the Canadian situation, and the case of law of Canada is replete with illustrations of our own courts' role in upholding the supremacy of the law. Maintenance of a vigilant, effective, informed and, above all, independent judiciary requires conscious care and attention on the part of the executive, the legislators and the judges themselves.
At the executive level of appointments to the judiciary, care must be taken to ensure the best qualified persons from the legal profession are attracted and appointed to the bench. In this regard, as I indicated in my first speech as Minister of Justice, I am carrying forward the tradition begun by my predecessor, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who in 1967 implemented the procedure of submitting names of candidates for judicial office to a committee of the Canadian Bar Associa-

tion to obtain its assessment of their suitability for appointment. None has been appointed without that assessment; none has been appointed without a favourable assessment.
I am grateful to those in the profession who are ready to come forward and serve as judges and be appointed pursuant to the Judges Act. I am grateful to those in the judiciary and those at the bar who have commented to me, since I have been Minister of Justice, on the quality and calibre of the people we have been able to put forward for judicial appointment.
I would like to emphasize that I am also committed to the appointment of judges who are sensitive and able to temper the law with compassion and common sense. In searching for such persons, I am conscious that these qualities are not the exclusive domain of either sex.

speechtext:
While the bench is now unrepresentative of the proportion of women in our country, this situation will change as more women graduate from law schools and become qualified with ten years practice at the bar for appointment. Even now, however, some progress is being made to redress the imbalance. In this regard, I take some pride in the appointment in Quebec of the first female chief justice and the appointment in Ontario of the first woman to the Canadian court of appeal. I hope they are signals of my intention to single out and to appoint to the bench, wherever possible, able women members of the bar.
The legislative arm of government, as represented by those of us in parliament, also has a key role to play in ensuring the high standards of our judiciary. Section 100 of the British North America Act charges parliament with fixing and providing for the salaries, allowances and pensions of federally appointed judges. It thus rests with us to ensure that the levels of remuneration and related benefits are sufficient to attract to the bench judges of the calibre of which I have been speaking.
In doing so, it is important to remember that the candidates we are seeking are the outstanding members of the profession, most often in the prime of their professional career with greater opportunity for advancement in private practice. While we, naturally, expect them to be prepared to make some sacrifice in assuming the public duty of judicial office, we must also offer them a level of compensation befitting the high office and heavy responsibility they are asked to assume. Similarly, we must provide that the size of the judiciary is commensurate with the workload which they have to handle.
To meet the pressures of the ever-growing number of civil and criminal cases coming before all levels of courts in the country-cases because of the law and the nature of the crime that are more complex and more time-consuming than ever before-the bill allows for the appointment of additional judges as requested by the provincial attorneys general. I underline, for the purposes of this debate, that no amendment increasing the size of a bench in any province is made without a firm request from the provincial attorney general.

speechtext:
I should emphasize, however, that the provincial attorneys general and I also recognize that adding judges is but one means of coping with the problem of growing case loads and consequent delays in the judicial system. That is why we, both federally and provincially, are currently engaged in actively exploring other measures to alleviate the problem which cannot simply be avoided by appointing more judges and building more court houses.
A number of the provinces are engaged in implementing modern management techniques in the operation of their courts, designed to provide a better case flow as outlined by the attorney general for Ontario in a white paper laid before that legislature some time ago. A number of courts are experimenting with revised procedures in civil and criminal cases that will cut down the length of preliminary inquiries and trials in Montreal, Ottawa and Vancouver, for example. Equally, at the federal level we are examining possible legislative measures which will reduce court delays at preliminary
Judges Act
inquiries and criminal trials, as well as means by which fewer minor offenders will be brought into the court system in the first place. I understand the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs will have a good deal to say about this in its forthcoming report. It is essential that these sorts of changes go hand in hand with appointing additional judges if we are to achieve the most efficient and effective use of the courts.
There have been questions in the House recently from the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) concerning unified family courts and the so-called reserve pool of judges. Under the bill there is a renewal of the reserve pool system-a system which was established by parliament in two rounds of amendments to the Judges Act made in 1973 under which a reserve pool was set up-so as to meet the anticipated requests from the provinces for additional judges during the next two years before the Judges Act was likely to be amended again. This pool is critical if we are to avoid delay in the appointment of new judges when these needs are identified and demonstrated by the provincial attorneys general.
Clause 18 of the bill also contains unique features in providing salaries for 15 judges who are specially designated for appointment to unified family courts. Under subclause (d), judges at the superior, county and district court level will be available for appointment at the request of the attorneys general as projects are established in the provinces. They will however-and this relates to a good question put by the hon. member for Calgary North-remain superior, county or district court judges. I consider this to be one of the more important provisions in the bill.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, I have been giving a very high priority to the establishment of unified family court pilot projects in a number of provinces. The existing fragmentation of jurisdiction forces families to take their family related problems to different judges. Thus, no one judge sees the entire family problem as a unit. In a unified family court all issues in a family law dispute can be determined by one judge in one court, with the help of support services. Such issues might include charges against minors, proceedings for the adoption, protection and guardianship of children, disputes respecting the matrimonial home, questions of divorce, separation and the custody of children. Support services for the courts would include family counselling and other services related to the resolution of family problems.
The establishment of unified family courts was one of the more important recommendations contained in the report on family law issued by the Law Reform Commission of Canada which I tabled in this House on May 4, 1976. Immediately following its tabling, it was discussed at a federal-provincial meeting of attorneys general in Vancouver hosted by me. There was general support and consensus among the 11 of us that we should endeavour to move toward the establishment of unified family courts in our respective jurisdictions on a test or pilot basis. By setting up pilot projects we will be able to assess
5318

May 5, 1977
Judges Act
the workability of the concept and to iron out some of the problems which are inherent in any major new initiative.
I am pleased to be able to report that agreement has already been reached to establish pilot projects in Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario and Newfoundland. In addition, the federal government has agreed to share in the cost of evaluating a pilot project which had previously been set up in British Columbia. It is my hope and, I am sure, the hope of all members, that we will be able to establish unified family courts on a permanent basis in a relatively short period of time, and that our reserve pool of judges for these courts will be fully utilized by the time the Judges Act next comes up for amendment.
Since I became Minister of Justice I have been deeply concerned about the degree of my department's involvement in the administration of judicial affairs. I believe that since the Department of Justice is responsible for the conduct of the government's litigation, it is preferable that the courts should not have to rely on the department for handling its administrative affairs. Again, it is a question of the principle of independence of the judiciary.
To remove the anomaly which currently exists-the anomaly of my department and my counsel often being the principal litigants before a court and also handling the administrative affairs of that court-I am recommending in this bill measures that will transfer from my department its administrative responsibilities for the federal courts and federally appointed judges. At the same time, we will preserve the principle of ministerial responsibility to parliament for the expenditure of public funds.
Under the proposed new regime there will be a commissioner for federal judicial affairs who will assume responsibility for all administrative affairs in respect of federally appointed judges; that is, the district, county and superior court judges and the federally constituted courts, the Federal Court of Canada and the Canadian Judicial Council, but excluding the Supreme Court of Canada. Under the Minister of Justice, the commissioner will have responsibility for the administration of judges' salaries, allowances and annuities, and for the budgetary, financial, personnel and operational requirements for the Federal Court and the Canadian Judicial Council.
I mentioned, Mr. Speaker, that I have excepted the Supreme Court of Canada. Given its unique status at the apex of the judicial system, the Supreme Court of Canada will have its registrar designated to perform these same functions in relation to that court and its members. At the same time, the registrar will be placed under the supervision of the chief justice, rather than the minister of justice, in carrying out the day to day administrative management of the court.
Further, amendments will be made to the Supreme Court Act relative to the publishing of reports, the management of the library and the management of the court, all in support of two principles; one removing the anomaly of my department being, on the one hand, the administrative arm of the court and, on the other hand, the chief litigant, and the other in support of the concept I touched upon at the beginning of my
(Mr. Bastard.]
speech, that we in the executive and in parliament should do all we can to enhance the independence of the judiciary.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to turn now to another critical area of this new bill, namely, the provisions relating to the Canadian Judicial Council. The council was established in 1971 to promote uniformity, efficiency and improvement in the quality of judicial services in the county, district and superior courts. To this end, the council is charged with responsibility for establishing conferences of chief justices and seminars for the continuing education of judges. Members of the House will also note that the act provides that the judicial council may establish an inquiry into the conduct of a judge and make a report to me and to parliament with regard to the rights of parliament under the British North America Act regarding the dismissal of judges.
In the intervening years the council has taken a number of important initiatives in these areas, including an innovative program of seminars for newly-appointed judges launched last year. Its continuing system of educational seminars is now firmly established and no doubt will be further developed in coming years. I also hope that the council will be able in the future to direct its attention to questions involving the application of modern management techniques to the operation of our courts, as well as means by which to reduce delays in court proceedings. The council is at present composed of the 24 chief justices of the superior courts, and its operation has, I believe, benefited from its small size. But at the same time, some of the council's activities are of direct interest to judges of the county and district courts which in many jurisdictions deal with most of the criminal cases in the area. I believe they should have an opportunity, namely, the judges of the county and district courts, for more direct involvement in the council's activities. In order to facilitate such participation without altering the present composition of the council, I am proposing in the bill the creation of a county court committee within the council.
This advisory committee will be composed of the chief judges and associate chief judges of the county and district courts, plus the senior judges nominated from those provinces where the courts have no chief judge, as in British Columbia. Thus, the committee will have a membership of ten, drawn from all provinces except Quebec and Prince Edward Island which have no county or district courts. The county court committee will be authorized to meet from time to time to discuss matters of common interest and concern in an effort to promote uniformity, efficiency and the quality of judicial service in the county and district courts. It will also be in a position to participate more directly in the planning and development of continuing educational seminars for the judges of the county and district courts. It is my hope that the establishment of this committee will bring about a closer working relationship between the judges of the superior, county and district court judges who all face many common problems and share many mutual interests.
May 5, 1977

Mr. Speaker, as I indicated earlier, judges' salaries can only be fixed by parliament, and it rests with parliament to ensure that these salaries are adequate properly to compensate for the heavy duties imposed upon those who accept appointment to judicial office. The bill provides for a two-stage increase in judges' salaries. The first increase of $2,000 would be retroactive to April 1, 1977, and the second, equal, increase would become effective on April 1, 1978. These increases are within the anti-inflation guidelines, averaging 4 per cent in 1977 and 3.8 per cent in 1978. The salaries were last set in 1975. It is not anticipated that the Judges Act will be amended for another two of three years, and therefore it is appropriate, I think, that parliament give this modest increase at this time rather than wait for another three years, which would be the earliest opportunity to make an adjustment since 1975.
Parliament is also charged with fixing and providing for the allowance paid to judges in carrying out their duties. 1 have already mentioned the importance I attach to judicial selfimprovement through participation by judges in seminars, conferences and meetings concerned with continuing legal education. Equally, I think it only proper that judges represent their courts at state and other official functions of the nation or of the bar. Such obligations do not fall upon all judges, of course, but they do fall, and understandably so, upon judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, chief justices and chief judges of all the other courts.
May I express my appreciation to members of the judiciary who in recent times, and certainly far more than in the past, are participating throughout the country in seminars, meetings of the bar and consultative sessions with the bar, much to the benefit of the judges themselves, of their courts, of the bar and of the law they administer. May I commend those judges who in terms of the continuing education program have put in an immense amount of hard work.
In this connection, the bill proposes to increase the conference allowance for judges of the Supreme Court of Canada to $1,000 per year and to provide these judges and the chief judges of the county and district courts with an annual representational allowance of $1,500. Many demands are placed upon Supreme Court judges to involve themselves in educational meetings and to represent our highest court at formal functions across the land. Equally, the chief judges of the county and district courts are in no different position than other heads of superior courts in being obliged to represent their courts. These amendments are necessary if the senior members of our judiciary are properly to discharge the judicial and extra-judicial responsibilities that fall upon them by virtue of the high office they hold and which, in my experience, they so willingly undertake.
I have endeavoured to outline the main features of Bill C-50. In conclusion, I would urge that parliament, in recognition of its role in relation to the independence of the judiciary, give close and early consideration to these amendments so they can be dealt with before parliament adjourns for the summer.

He would have nothing to do with the administration of the case lists. That continues to be a judicial function. The proposal for a commissioner does not affect any judicial functions of any of the judges. Obviously, in our parliamentary system the commissioner would be a deputy head reporting to me, and I to parliament; but that whole function of my department would be moved to the office of the commissioner.
With regard to section 96 judges-federally appointed judges not of federally constituted courts-the function of the commissioner would be to deal with pensions, travelling allowances, leave of absence, moving allowances and that type of matter.

speechtext:
I thank the minister for his clarification. I wanted that point cleared up because I did not want a new officer set up who would interfere with the independence of the courts.
First of all, I want to congratulate the minister on his address this afternoon in setting out, in particular, the functions of the judiciary and how the separation of power operates in our democratic system. Some years ago the British parliament instigated a study concerning the independence of the judiciary. I was pleased to hear the minister speak of the independence of the judiciary, because not long ago in this chamber we learned that some in responsible positions had interfered with judges in a certain province, either deliberately or otherwise. It was alleged that that interference affected
800t2-S8y2

May 5, 1977
Judges Act
ministers and other members of this House. I say, Mr. Speaker, that in a democratic system an independent judiciary is most important.
Before I comment on the minister's speech, let me congratulate him and the members of his department on the fine calibre of men and women they have appointed to the bench in this country in recent years. The minister is to be congratulated especially for the appointments he has made in Alberta. Alberta appointments have been based on the calibre of the lawyer rather than the political affiliation of the appointee. By so doing the minister has taken a step in the direction recommended by the Canadian Bar Association and other bar associations, and the end result will be judges of ever higher calibre. I felt obliged to put those comments on record since I have been speaking of the independence of the judiciary.
In the study previously alluded to, involving a review by parliament and the courts of judges in Great Britain and the United States, the importance of the independence of judges was emphasized. The study said that the independent judiciary should guarantee the security of the weak against the strong and the individual against the community. It should present a shield against the tyranny of power and arrogance, and against the irresponsibility and irrationality of popular action. Always, the underlying, basic assumption is the intellectual and moral integrity of the judicial officer in his pronouncements.
It is well recognized that the courts must always assure society that the weak will be protected from the strong and that the individual will be protected from the all-powerful state. Actually, lawyers should consider themselves as social engineers. It is the function of the lawyer, of the legal profession, to make sure that the individual is protected from the all-powerful state. What happens to an individual if he is charged with an offence, or engages the state in civil litigation either at the federal or provincial level? The state, with the country's tax money at its disposal, can hire the best experts and finest counsel. It is the job of the lawyer acting for the individual to protect that individual from the all-powerful state and make sure that he is fairly and squarely dealt with by the independent judiciary. That is the function of the lawyer. It is the function of bar associations to be responsible for the conduct of, indeed to discipline, the lawyer.
In each province lawyers are governed by the provincial professional act. The professional act allows lawyers to set up their own bar association which sets out guidelines and conditions according to which men and women are called to the bar. If defalcation takes place, the bar association will discipline the lawyer concerned and take other remedies necessary. I know that the bill speaks of lawyers with ten or more years' experience being appointed to the bench. They need many years of experience in practice if they are to carry out their purposes and functions in the manner I outlined at the beginning of my remarks.
Mr. Speaker, for a number of years I have been a member of the Alberta and Saskatchewan bar associations, and I can

say that we are justly proud in Canada of the high quality of men and women who have been appointed to the judiciary, appointed to protect the rights of Canadians everywhere in this country. I say this in all sincerity.
Let me now deal with another point about which I am concerned. On page 3 of the bill there is provision for the appointment of additional judges to our superior, county, district and appellate courts. The chief justices and attorneys general of the provinces submit recommendations to the Minister of Justice or the department. The Minister of Justice, as he accurately and properly said, acts on the basis of those recommendations in the appointment of judges, and in so doing acts according to the laws and constitution of this country. In this connection I draw the attention of the House to page 11 of the bill which provides for the appointment of 15 judges who shall deal with family court matters. However, I see no evidence to suggest that the Minister of Justice has made agreements with the provinces, as it is the responsibility of the provinces to create such family courts.
For several decades the dockets of our high courts and superior courts have been flooded with divorce cases. This created a great deal of work for judges and held up the disposition of civil and sometimes criminal cases. Long lists of divorce cases were the bane of our superior courts. After the divorce laws were changed, our courts were forced to deal with an even greater work load because more people wanted to be divorced. According to recent statistics, Canadian divorce rates are as high as those in the United States.
I have always felt that our federal system of law has not been quite fair to divorced Canadian females with children. Let me illustrate what happens in a divorce. As part of the divorce proceedings, a judge, say in Manitoba, Alberta or Saskatchewan, can make an order for the maintenance of the children of the marriage or alimony for the spouse. The ex-husband may be well employed and a man of means. If he moves to another province, the court may lose jurisdiction and the order may not be enforced. Surely it is up to marriage partners to fulfil the first responsibilities of their marriage, the provision for the welfare of their family. As I say, if the husband moves from Alberta, say, to another province, unless there is a proper reciprocal agreement between the provinces the order made in Alberta is not enforceable.
In addition, any attempt to enforce such orders is costly. It costs a great deal of money to hire lawyers and other legal costs are very high as well. Mr. Speaker, hundreds of thousands of women in this country have suffered over the years because they were not able to enforce maintenance orders and so provide for the necessities and education of their young children. As the Minister of Justice knows, he being a lawyer from British Columbia, unless there are unusual circumstances the judge awards custody of young children to the mother. Therefore, the mother must provide for the necessities and education of her young children.
If she is on welfare, the taxpayer must bear the cost. On the other hand, the husband may be earning an adequate salary, but because of the present state of our law he is able to evade
May 5, 1977

his responsibilities. I hope the Minister of Justice can meet with the ministers of all ten provinces and propose enabling legislation to be passed in this House and in the provincial legislatures which will provide uniform law right across this country. Only then will orders made in Alberta or Ontario be enforced in other parts of Canada. We need such law to make sure that our young do not suffer from the irresponsibility of one of their parents.
That is my recommendation today. I hope that when the minister does set up these family courts-and I realize it is the function of the provinces to set them up-that matter is taken into consideration. I would have thought, and I say this kindly to the minister, we would have had an agreement at least with the provinces if we are, indeed, setting up these family courts. All the bill does is set up a pool of judges: it appoints extra judges to the superior courts. Under most of the jurisdictions that I know, and there are some exceptions such as Ontario, the jurisdiction over divorce, making orders for alimony and maintenance and dealing with domestic matters is under the Queen's Bench or superior courts, the trial divisions of the various provinces.
What we are doing is adding more judges. These judges will be trying those cases anyway. What the minister had in mind, and what the Speech from the Throne was dealing with was that we would have a county court like we have in district courts, the trial supreme court and an appeal court, and a separate and distinct court set up for family matters so that cases could be expedited and orders made and enforced across the land. It would deal with those matters that are cluttering up the courts.
I cannot think of anything more monotonous than a judge spending a couple of days listening to 30 or 40 divorce cases, especially when the only ground is adultery. They listen to that kind of evidence hour after hour and day after day. I cannot think of anything more monotonous for a man skilled in the law than listening to that trash while other cases are held in abeyance. The place for domestic problems should be the family court. Those courts should be empowered to make orders which would be enforced across the country. I do not think I can put it any more clearly than that.
I commend the minister for his action on the question of salaries. Young lawyers only at the bar a few years often make more than the chief justice of the province. If you are going to continue to have high calibre, intelligent men, we must keep salaries at least within the ball-park of what they could earn in other occupations. On the face of it, an increase of $2,000 sounds like quite a large sum. However, when you add it to what they are making at the present time, and take into consideration the scale of income tax, they are lucky to take home an extra $800 or $900. Remember that judges cannot write off expenses which can be written off in a law practice. The tax is deducted at source. It is like members of parliament: when we get our cheques, they have taken off the allowance for our pension and our tax. This increase is certain-
Judges Act
ly not out of line. It has been two or three years since we last examined judges' salaries. If we are to have the kind of men that the minister and I discussed, we must compensate them so they can have the degree of independence that is necessary for the judiciary to function as it does.
I have tried to keep my remarks brief. I endorse the bill. We will be supporting it. I congratulate the minister for bringing it in at this time.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE TIME SPENT AS MAGISTRATE IN DETERMINING ELIGIBILITY FOR SENIOR POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one thing about the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford): when it comes to the political field he is fiercely competitive and very partisan in his politics. When it comes to the administration of his duties as Minister of Justice, he is able, articulate, efficient and fair. I have to say that about the Minister of Justice. The same could be said for some of the other ministers of justice. I notice that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is in the chamber. When he was minister of justice he had the administrative ability to do, and in fact did, an excellent job in that field.
This bill is non-controversial. All that members have to do is try to improve some of the provisions that are contained in it. Bill C-50 deals with four areas: first, the appointment of additional judges; second, increased salaries for judges; third, changes to the Canadian Judicial Council; and fourth, the appointment of a commissioner who will take over some of the administrative duties which fell within the Department of Justice. What we have to do is improve some of the provisions contained in the bill. I may premise that by saying it is the duty of all of us to humanize the law. Judges and lawyers play a very important part in humanizing the law.
It has been said that the law should move from the people to the judges. In the past there has been a great separation between judges and ordinary folk. In my years of practice I have had many cases where people were literally terrified of going to court. They were overwhelmed and overawed by the presence of the judge in the courtroom. That imposes a detachment, a separation of the people from the law. Therefore, it is very important that we humanize the law and get lawyers and judges participating in going to the people in attitude concerning the law.
I have noticed many changes in the law since coming to this place 12 years ago. They are all for the better. I think of the Law Reform Commission and the work they did in setting forth some of the problems and suggesting solutions. They have not been picked up completely by our ministers of justice, but we are moving in the right direction. I think, too, of some of the amendments to the Criminal Code, especially the change with regard to absolute and conditional discharge. That was a good move in changing the law.
I caught some of the adjectives that the minister used concerning judges. I think he said they have to be sensitive and able. I would say they have to be learned, independent, impartial, fair and compassionate. I recall the Hon. John Turner, when he was minister of justice, summing it up in very few words: he said they have to be compassionate and possess

May 5, 1977
Judges Act
common sense. That is the real mark of a judge, and that is what we have to strive for in our appointments.
I have said there has been a separation and detachment by lawyers and judges with regard to ordinary folk which has terrified many people with regard to cases before the courts. One thing we could do is improve the jargon with regard to courts. As hon. members know, in the Supreme Court we have to address the judge as "your lordship" or "my lord". In the county court it is "your honour". At one time in magistrates' courts it was "your worship". Now we have changed "your worship" to "your honour". It seems to me that the terms "your lordship" or "my lord" do not play an important part in the courts today. We might, instead, simply use the designation "your honour" when addressing a judge. It is a little warmer. It is more meaningful than the term "my lord" or "your lordship". This is something the Minister of Justice can think through.
The reason we are appointing additional judges is that the courts face a very heavy case load. A multiplicity of court cases has arisen in the last 10 or 15 years. This is the result of the increase in population and to some extent, no doubt, because of the changes which were made in the divorce laws. Then, again, people may be becoming more contentious. One way in which we could reduce the court case load, more especially in the province of Ontario, would be by taking motor vehicle cases out of the courts. In some provinces-for example, in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba- they have already been removed from the jurisdiction of the courts and made subject to the rulings of tribunals.
In Ontario there is a very heavy list, and on examining that list you notice it includes a tremendous number of cases involving motor vehicles. I see that in its speech from the throne the government of Quebec indicated an intention to take motor vehicle cases out of the courts. This might well be done in Ontario; the number of judges needed would then be fewer.
The minister touched on the qualities and qualifications needed by judges. He pointed out that women are now being appointed to county courts, family courts and courts of appeal. This is an excellent trend, though at the moment I would have to say it is tokenism; there is not the balance there should be. I hope we can move away from tokenism to a situation in which there is real representation of women in the composition of the courts.
Ours is a very complex society. One of the best illustrations of this is the appointment of 15 judges to take care of a unified family court system. Pilot projects are going on in connection with the establishment of family courts, and I think they have proven to be a success. The minister is moving in the right direction when he co-operates with the province to provide more judges as an essential part of the development of a unified family court system. It is most frustrating for people who find themselves in domestic disputes to discover they must go to different courts for decisions about the various issues

which arise. For example, with regard to custody they sometimes go to the family court, sometimes to the surrogate court and sometimes to the supreme court. With regard to maintenance, sometimes they go to family court and sometimes to the supreme court. In connection with grounds for divorce, sometimes there is an option of going to the supreme court or to the county court. The decision to unify the system and to have all these matters presented, debated and resolved before one court is a wise one.
I have talked about the complexity of courts, more especially of the supreme court and the county court. If one were to analyse the various functions of the supreme court and the county court, one would find there was very little difference in the performance of those duties. The minister should take a deep and considered look at the advisability of combining both the county court and the supreme court to one court. This would avoid the confusion which prevails at the moment as to whether people should commence their actions in one court or the other.
I recall when the Minister of Transport was minister of justice. I spoke to him with regard to this question and I think he was in agreement, in principle, to the idea of combining the county courts and the supreme courts. I am sure that the former minister and the present minister Find very little difference with regard to performance of the duties involved. It is important that we should seek to end the separation which adds to the confusion and to the detachment of judges.
When one considers the changes in the composition of the Canadian Judicial Council-the minister says that to recognize the county court judges, a county court committee will be set up-we become aware of the differences which exist between the supreme court and the county court. I say that these differences should not prevail. It seems to me that the Judicial Council is fulfilling an important and effective role with regard to judges. The holding of educational seminars by judges is, in my opinion, a step in the right direction. However, a move to combine the county courts and the supreme court would be a far better step to take.
I should like the minister to advise us further with regard to the functions of the judicial council. It seems to me the council arose following the Landreville case. Mr. Justice Landreville was in a very difficult position, and in order to oust him it was necessary to bring forward a motion both in this House and in the Senate. In the event, the judge resigned and no motion was necessary. But as a result of that case the Canadian Judicial Council was formed with responsibilities in the field of education and of discipline.
I think we in Canada can be very proud of the performance of our judges. They are to be complimented. The high standard is probably due in part to the process followed in making appointments. I think their performance has been excellent. But would the minister advise me what the powers of the council are with regard to discipline? My own opinion is that the complaints felt by individuals should be brought before the judicial council. Those who complain against judges should be given a hearing on the basis of which recommendations should
May 5, 1977

be made to the Minister of Justice who should have power to ask a judge to resign where this seems appropriate.
I said earlier that ours is a very complex society. I notice that the chief justice of the high court of Ontario made a statement to reporters recently with regard to class actions. He was afraid that class actions would take time in the courts and that they could add to delays and possibly to confusion.
Class actions had their origin in the United States where groups of people joined together to bring an action regarding an injury they had suffered. The best example I can give in Canada is the "rusty Fords" action. Many people who bought Ford motor cars a few years ago got a very bad deal; in no time at all the cars had rusted. The problem was to bring a class action which would be successful. Hon. members can appreciate the problems of a class action. Somebody has to initiate it; they have to get together the people who have been aggrieved; they have to retain counsel; they have to present evidence; and in many cases a good deal of expert evidence is required. In the "rusty Fords" case there were difficulties in developing the action, and the compensation offered by the Ford Motor Company amounted to little or nothing.
Class actions are becoming a very important aspect of our law, both from the consumer and from the environmental point of view, and we have to assist in the promotion and performance of such actions. The minister must see to it that we have the proper number of judges and that the courts are not cluttered up with cases. I repeat to the minister, as I am sure he knows full well, that in Ontario the number of motor vehicle cases brought is astronomical and they are responsible for cluttering up the courts. When a law professor analysed some of the motor vehicle cases and their result in the courts, he found that sometimes because of lack of proper presentation the litigants had suffered considerably.
The Law Reform Commission has brought forth many studies regarding diversionary procedures in criminal cases and other cases. I hope the Minister of Justice will adopt some of the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission on the question of diversionary procedures and thus cut down the case load of criminal actions. I note that the minister is attempting at this time to streamline some of the rules concerning evidence. I think he should give an equal amount of time and attention to some diversionary procedures which could be adopted, and thus help the situation.
There is a tremendous amount of specialization on these days, and perhaps we in Canada should develop specialized courts. We are moving in the right direction in regard to family courts. In regard to bankruptcy we do have specialized courts. Perhaps we have to move further regarding specialization in other fields of law. They have done this in England where judges with wide experience in the law are appointed to a particular branch, and they do an excellent job. I think it is almost asking the impossible to have a judge learned in all fields of the law today. It is just too much to expect them to be
Judges Act
expert in criminal law, corporate law and all the other branches of the law.
The minister has cleared up the administrative duties of the commissioner, and I am sure this is a step in the right direction. As I said at the beginning, this is a non-controversial bill. What we have to do is humanize the law. I hope that the Minister of Justice starts this process with lawyers and judges and brings forth many measures having to do with amendments to the Criminal Code and other acts, and thus humanize the law. Then we can proudly say that we have the best judicial system and the best laws which apply to all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE TIME SPENT AS MAGISTRATE IN DETERMINING ELIGIBILITY FOR SENIOR POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a most statesmanlike debate and I will try and make my remarks in the same spirit, though it is going to be a struggle. This is a welcome piece of legislation and appears to be a good step forward. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) has, I think, a good reputation. I have a little irritation with him, which I will come to in a few minutes, but first of all I am glad to have the opportunity to speak in this debate since I am the only barrister and solicitor present in this chamber from the province of Newfoundland and Labrador.
It is amazing that out of the seven Newfoundland members there is only one lawyer, which is indeed a setback to human progress. There are very few provinces with only one lawyer among their membership in the House of Commons. As everyone knows, usually the House of Commons and houses of assembly have a large number of lawyers as members, but coming from Newfoundland I feel rather lonely. Even the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) has no training in law, though he is certainly getting quite a bit of training in external affairs.
As one grows older, Mr. Speaker, one can usually see that one is getting older because the policemen start looking very young and judges become your contemporaries. A recent appointment by the Minister of Justice to the Newfoundland supreme court, Mr. Justice Noel Goodridge, is a boyhood friend of mine. I grew up with him. He has been on the bench now for only one year. He is a first-class judge on the bench of Newfoundland and he will be a tremendous adornment to the bench there. Other judges recently appointed were people I have known from boyhood, and this really shows me that time is passing on. When you see that some of your brother lawyers with whom you came to the bar are now on the bench, you know that you are getting over the hill. But I certainly wish them well, and I know that they will do very well on the bench, where they will be sitting for the next 30 years until reaching retirement age.
I should also like to mention what a fine appeal court we had in Newfoundland when I was a young lawyer. I should just like to put the names of the court on the record. There was the then chief justice, the late Sir Albert Walsh. Then there was the late Sir Brian Dunfield, and the late Harry Winter. They were three Newfoundland judges of the very highest calibre who were understanding when a young lawyer first came before them. They were men of high integrity and intelligence and a real adornment to the bench. I know that

May 5, 1977
Judges Act
our present judiciary are all following in their footsteps. It was a pleasure to appear before men of that nature, particularly the chief justice, the late Sir Albert Walsh, who was a great judicial scholar and humanitarian.
I should like the Minister of Justice to try to deal with one matter respecting the bench. We know that the Canadian Judicial Council is supposed to have the task these days of trying to deal with disciplinary questions concerning judges, but there is one area which is not so much a matter of discipline in the sense of a judge misbehaving or a judge behaving in a way which might require a resolution by the House of Commons and the Senate. I refer to the small number of judges who are very slow in their work and in bringing down judgments. They will hear a case, and I have known of cases where three years later judgment had not been rendered. That is a very serious matter, because justice delayed is justice denied. Therefore, I would like the minister to deal with this matter. It is an awkward area because, as we all know, our judges must be left with their independence. We cannot have executive interference with judges in their role as judges.
The government must consider the rights of the litigants who appear and whose cases are before judges. The cases may involve them in a great deal of money while waiting for a judgment. It is going to cost one side or the other a great deal of money. Perhaps in other areas humanitarian or human relationship factors are involved. I believe the situation to be intolerable where a judge can go longer than six months or, at the very maximum, a year before he brings down a judgment. I do not know whether the minister can give some direction as to what can be done about this problem, or whether the Canadian Judicial Council has been asked, or will be asked, to do something about it. It is a serious and awkward problem for the bench, for the bar and for the administration of justice. It is a problem that requires a device to be arrived at so that those kinds of rare situations can be avoided.
I approve of the attempts the minister is making to do something about family law within the new concept of family law courts, courts which will deal with all aspects of families- divorce, separation, custody of children, and so on. There is no other area of the law with which I have had any experience that is more trying, has more human values involved and a more human story involved. It has the capability of causing human beings pain and sorrow. I am referring to matters that come up before judges dealing with family law. Custody of children, in particular, is an area that is very much the stuff with which human sorrow is concerned. There is also the attempt by one parent or the other to use their children to get revenge on the other party. These are the kinds of cases that are very difficult for judges to deal with.
These cases are much better dealt with by judges whose experience is totally within the field of family life. They are, therefore, spending their time in that kind of human situation and they understand it. They also have the court's resources to

try to deal with it in a humanitarian and common sense way. I believe the move the minister is making is in the right direction. He has a suggested agreement with the province of Newfoundland, and three or four other provinces are interested.
Judges who are ordinarily dealing with commercial and criminal matters are very often not suited to dealing with very subtle relationships between people. I never make any judgment on family matters. The only family matter that one can really make a judgment on is one you are involved in yourself. What the relationship is between two other people is very difficult for outsiders to fathom. This is an area where a lot of expertise and understanding is needed. This is a move in the right direction and I approve of it.
While I have the chance, I want to say that the administration of justice is certainly not uniform across Canada. Constitutional jurisdiction over matters of the judicial system are divided between the federal government and the provincial governments. As all members of the House know, the federal government appoints the judges, pays their salaries and a portion of their expenses. The provinces are responsible for the administration of justice. They are responsible for paying the expenses of the courts, the staff that belong to the courts, building courthouses, and the like. That falls within the responsibility of the provincial governments, with the exception of the Federal Court of Canada and the Supreme Court of Canada. That is all well and good.
All of us in this chamber know there are provinces well endowed with resources, and provinces that are less endowed financially. I do not believe significant recognition in the administration of justice in Canada has been taken of that fact. For example, the facilities in the system of what used to be called magistrates' court-today called provincial courts in Newfoundland-can by no stretch of the imagination be compared to the same system in Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta or practically any other province. The magistrates and provincial court judges of the provincial courts in Newfoundland have the most primitive facilities in which to operate. Those magistrates are now called judges, but I will use the word "magistrates" so that you will know who I am talking about. The magistrates do not have a shorthand-typist in their court to take evidence. They do not have proper court facilities. The hon. gentleman who sits in this House representing Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) will verify that fact.
A lot of money needs to be spent in the province of Newfoundland on court facilities for the supreme court of Newfoundland, for the district courts and for the magistrates' courts which are now called provincial courts. The government of Newfoundland does not have the wherewithal to do that. I have not checked this for some two or three months, but I think the case still is that the judges of the supreme court of Newfoundland do not even have dictating and transcribing equipment. They have to dictate their judgments to stenographers. I do not think each of them has a stenographer.
The same stenographers who take down the evidence in court and who have to transcribe the evidence for appeals will
May 5, 1977

also type judgments for the judges and do their correspondence. This is an inefficient and shocking situation, to my mind. The province of Newfoundland has limited financial resources. It has not the resources to go and build a proper system of court houses and court buildings that are needed in St. John's and outside of St. John's. They are certainly needed outside of St. John's, because at least St. John's has the supreme court and the district court offices which are in half-decent buildings, and facilities which are not too bad. Outside of St. John's the situation is very much worse.
Therefore, we do not have an equal system of justice across Canada. That is because we do not have the same facilities across Canada. That is why I suggest to the government of Canada and to the minister that steps should be taken to try to correct this situation. I know the province of Newfoundland has made submissions to the government of Canada. The minister of justice for Newfoundland and the attorney general, the Hon. T. A. Hickman, Q.C., has put forward suggestions to the government of Canada that they share some responsibility for meeting the costs of the administration of justice in that province. That is one area where I can see the government of Canada, in any constitutional rearrangement, taking over more responsibility, and not less.
Unfortunately, our financial system does not follow the system of the division of power, as every member of this House knows. There are all kinds of cost-sharing programs, but 1 do not think we have any cost-sharing programs in the administration of justice. Penitentiaries are another area, but they are not quite covered by this bill.
We have to move, in Canada, toward increased federal financial responsibility for the administration of justice. Appointing judges and paying them is not enough. The government of Canada should be interested in seeing that they have the proper facilities to do their work equally well wherever they are in Canada. A judge should not suffer from inferior facilities if he sits in Newfoundland or Prince Edward Island as compared to here in Ontario. That is just as important as health and just as important as welfare. The system of justice is equally important.
I have not practiced much since 1966 because I became involved in the political business, but I am glad to note that the quality of lawyers being turned out today is very high. I am also glad to note that law schools are more aware of their responsibility to the public generally and to the public interest. More people who are taking law are interested in aspects of public law and not just interested in becoming lawyers to earn a fantastic living. A lawyer, of course, can still earn a good living. There has been a vast increase in the number of lawyers in Newfoundland. Now they have to start getting out around the province and cannot all stay in St. John's and Corner Brook. They have to go to Grand Falls, Gander and Marys-town to bring legal services to places where they were never received or available before.
One of the things dealt with in this bill is the Supreme Court of Canada. As hon. gentlemen may know, there is a matter now pending before the Supreme Court of Canada in
Judges Act
which I am talking an interest. I am taking an interest in it because I am interested in seeing justice being done in Canada equally for everyone.
Yesterday I asked the Minister of Justice a question about a situation that cries out for explanation. I asked how the government can have a case pending before the Supreme Court of Canada for about seven years and do nothing, that I know of, to see that it is brought on and decided one way or the other. The appeal should either be heard or dismissed. I want to know how that case can be allowed to lie there since 1970.
Mr. Speaker, I am referring to the reported case of Doyle v. M.N.R. relating to the tax years 1950 and 1954, which is 24 and 27 years ago. Just imagine, the court is still being asked to decide issues that occurred 24 and 27 years ago! Events that occurred in 1950 and 1954 were not heard by the Income Tax Appeal Board until 1967, and then they were heard and decided in the exchequer court in 1970, three years later. That is bad enough, but the taxpayer who was found liable by the exchequer court in 1970 for a huge amount of taxes then appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1970 and has been permitted to let the appeal lie there until now. This matter demands an explanation, and if I do not get one I will raise the matter in this House on every possible occasion as long as I am here.
There is one thing about me, Mr. Speaker; I am persistent. The Minister of Justice is going to discover that I am persistent and stubborn. I am going to get to the bottom of this matter. I asked that question of the Minister of Justice yesterday in the House. I wrote to him on March 23 and on April 22, and after I spoke in this House on April 21 I wrote to the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin). I thought I would write first because I might have to raise the matter again in the House. After three or four weeks going by without an answer, I did bring it up in the House again and I will continue to do so until members are sick of hearing about it and until what happened has been explained and why extraordinarily lenient treatment should be extended to any taxpayer, least of all one who does not deserve it.
Yesterday I asked a question relating to the Supreme Court of Canada. I asked the minister to bring us up to date on what action was taken to rectify this situation. As reported at page 5273 of Hansard the minister answered that he had reviewed the proceedings in these matters with his officials, and went on to say:
They have been proceeding at a pace that the rules of the court allow-
We all know that the rules of the court allow delay if both parties agree, Mr. Speaker. The minister continued:
-except in one case where adjournment was agreed to from the winter list of the Supreme Court of Canada to the spring list, which should result in that case being heard in the spring of this year. Briefly, the officers of my department are instructed, and have been for some time, to proceed with these matters as fast as the rules of the court allow.

May 5, 1977
Judges Act
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the rules of the court do not have the least thing to do with the gross negligence which has apparently occurred in the matter. The rules of the court do not say you must delay seven years before proceeding with an income tax case against John C. Doyle. The rules are there to govern. You put in a factum and then you have so many days after the person responds, etc., but the implication here is that the matter has been held over seven years because of the Supreme Court of Canada. I say that is not the reason; it is not an acceptable reason, and it is an unfair criticism of the Supreme Court of Canada.
As a supplementary question I asked if the Minister of Justice was suggesting that the Supreme Court of Canada was lax in hearing cases involving taxes, and if a seven-year delay was normal and in accordance with the rules of the court in cases regarding income tax. The minister replied:
No. Of course, the Supreme Court of Canada deals with its cases diligently and as fast as it possibly can.
Certainly it does when the lawyers bring a case before it, but if the lawyers on both sides are satisfied to let the matter lie, like shaving soap-it does not sink and does not float, but just lies there-then, of course, the court cannot deal with it expeditiously because the parties do not care if it is ever settled. This will not wash, Mr. Speaker. There is not one comma or full stop in the rules of the Supreme Court of Canada to justify this matter being allowed to lie there for seven years.
I went to the trouble of finding out how many appeals on income tax matters are before the Supreme Court of Canada at the present time. I am advised that as of March 31, 1977, there were ten. One appeal has been heard and they are awaiting judgment, but the other nine appeals have yet to be dealt with by the court. Of those nine, presumably two are the cases I mentioned, Doyle v. M.N.R. in 1950 and 1954, so that leaves seven cases. What I am going to get next, unless the minister wants to get it for me, is the date the other appeals were allowed, and for what income tax year. Are they for 1950 and 1954? When were the appeals first entered? How many appeals are pending going back to 1950 and 1954?
The other day I came across the case of a man I know in British Columbia. The income tax people allege that he owes $23,000 for the last couple of years-not $1,859,000 from 1954. He is not a fugitive from justice; he is not in Panama and has not been to Costa Rica. He is in Canada and is alleged to owe the Department of National Revenue $23,000. The department tells him that he has to pay the $23,000 and pay the interest on it before he can appeal. Yet we have this other person who has owed millions of dollars for years and years and is wanted in Canada to face charges of fraud. But still the Department of Justice and the Department of National Revenue do not move, and I want to know why. Before I am finished, the people of Canada will want to know why, as well, and they are going to get an answer. I know these things take time. They take time in Newfoundland. You ask a question one year, you keep asking and asking and eventually the media

picks up its pencil and looks into the matter. The next thing you know is that it is a major issue and an election turns on it.
I am genuinely disturbed by this case, Mr. Speaker, and I am going to get to the bottom of it. The Minister of Justice made a mistake yesterday when he tried to slough me off with the answer that this had something to do with the rules of the Supreme Court of Canada. If by some chance it had, then we should ask the Supreme Court to change the rules. I should say I have every confidence in those gentlemen of the Supreme Court of Canada.
I said at the beginning that I wanted to be statesmanlike, Mr. Speaker, so I have not allowed myself to get excited. If this debate had not been on a high level, I would have gone wild on this subject. I am holding that for the time when the amendments to the Income Tax Act come before the House; but when anything remotely associated with National Revenue or Justice comes up, I will introduce this matter. I will leave the subject for now, however.
I just make the point to the Minister of Justice that I think he is going to have to make a statement on motions, or somehow in this House, and go into this matter in detail to try to persuade the House it is not a case of gross negligence or malfeasance, misfeasance or whatever-feasance. We are all going to be treated the same in Canada when it comes to paying taxes, paying the interest and paying for security. The law is for us all. A fugitive from justice should not get preferential treatment. As a matter of fact, a fugitive from justice should get tougher treatment. If you do not pay your taxes, you are a citizen, you live here, you work here, and you have a business here, they are knocking on your door with warrants, they are seizing your assets, they are putting on attachments-

speechtext: Language!

Mr. Speaker, by most standards I should not enter this debate because I am not a lawyer, but I want to say a few words on this bill because of a particular case with which I am dealing which is related to family courts. The matter also involves what is alleged to be an international kidnapping. I think the case was well publicized in the newspapers of this country last year. Briefly, it is this: a Canadian citizen married a man from Iran who was given landed immigrant status and subsequently fathered her child, also a Canadian citizen.
This gentleman then went to the Iranian embassy and registered his wife and his child as Iranian citizens. A short time later he separated from his wife, a divorce was granted and the courts of Ontario gave the wife custody of the child. The husband was gone for six years from Canada; he went back to Iran. Under the court order, the wife had custody of the child. There was some correspondence back and forth in which he demanded that the child be sent to Iran to visit him. The judge of the circuit court of Ontario looked into the details of the case and advised the wife against sending the
Adjournment Motion
child to Iran because apparently under Iranian law she was a Iranian citizen.
The husband returned to Canada and under order of the court had visiting privileges from nine to six in the daytime. He visited the home, took the child with him, boarded a taxi, went to Montreal and boarded an aeroplane for New York. From New York he went to Paris, London and then to Teheran. The distraught mother called the RCMP, and they said, "We cannot deal with it because it is a family court matter". Subsequently she called the FBI. They were not able to deal with it because they did not have a request from the RCMP. Then she called Scotland Yard in London, England, who agreed that if they came in contact with the child they would detain her so that her status could be clarified. The point here is that here is a woman and a child who are Canadian citizens and who have had their citizenship denied them. The woman considered going to Iran but was advised against it because she was an Iranian citizen by the mere fact of her husband going to the embassy and registering her that way.
What I would like the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to look into is whether in such cases-and there are several of them-our embassies overseas can make representations to the courts in the other country so that this matter can be adjudicated.
There are human considerations here. The young girl in question, who is 11 years old, has contacted her mother by telephone and by letter in which she made heart-rending comments such as, "I am fighting for my life. Please help". I am not being critical of our Department of External Affairs.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, on November 25, 1976, quite a long time ago, I was speaking on that subject when the House adjourned on that famous Bill C-1001; it was just given a large figure and that is all. Bill C-1001 tends to incorporate the Continental Bank of Canada, thus making of the Industrial Acceptance Corporation a chartered bank. This bill that was studied and passed by the Senate, since only money bills concern that hon. Chamber, has not been passed so far.
On November 25, 1976, that bill was again deferred. But its Liberal sponsors, undaunted, came back before the House on February 3, 1977, and were defeated once again. Today, the same bill is rising again from its ashes and returns once again to haunt the House of Commons. It is strange that when money bills are involved, they can be brought back time and again during the private members' hour, mind you, as long as the opposition is not winded enough to allow to pass the measures they want to get through. If it can be said that the judiciary has a wide influence, it can also be said that the financial power is still quite alive and that its servants must conquer or die. In our system of government, which depends on high finance, it is the only way for a political party to survive. You have to grovel before powerful bankers and give them whatever they want. And that is indeed what the two old parties do.
And today even the New Democratic Party is giving up. While listening to the hon. member a moment ago, I was asking myself a lot of questions and wondering how much IAC will have to pay to gain the approval of the three other parties. This is a question we intend to ask in committee, for this bill is finally going to be referred to the committee. I have been sitting in this House for 15 years now and I have seen many
May 5, 1977

finance bills of this kind, which deal only with money. We have to stop burying our heads in the sand. People know very well that those bills are not passed for nothing, let us be frank.
That is why I oppose this one energetically. I see smiles, because we dare not tell the truth to the people, but they are not that stupid. They know what it costs those companies to create a bank. Everybody has long since been aware of what goes on behind the scene. We are discussing bank legislation and it has to profit someone. That is it! In my opinion, it has to profit someone, for ever since 1 have sat here it has always profited the party in power.
As the saying goes, business is business. And they claim to defend the interests of the people. That is what revolts me most, when I hear them say: "the interests of the people". Imagine! To create one more bank, to strengthen monopolies, that is the goal. Yet they talk about competition. Let no one tell me there is competition among banks. It is the worst monopoly in the country. Today, through the establishment of this bank, we reinforce that monopoly-
