Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to say one thing: every time I speak, the hon. member intervenes without rhyme or reason. He does not repeat what I have said but makes up statements of his own. I suspect he feels the hat fits him or his party. However, to come back to what he said, he did not quote me, but made up remarks of his own. It would have been better for him not to speak up and to sit quietly, as he usually does, and remain silent than to blunder as he did. Mr. Speaker, I was merely denouncing the monopoly of the banks which today are not controlled efficiently but in fact control the governments. That is what I object to at this time.
Continental Bank of Canada
Mr. Speaker, we have many arguments to put forward. I have just been handed a statement made by the Prime Minister. I quote:
We must start by doing away with the power of money which has a vested interest in keeping the status quo. The banks are the most generous contributors to the two funds, Conservative and Liberal. Obviously, they consider their donations as insurance premiums against any form of radicalism.
Mr. Speaker, we have a lot more quotations like that. A while ago, I said we will have to quit burying our heads in the sand. The young member who has come to the House will certainly learn that. I believe he has been digging a hole for a long time in which he wants to hide his head, but let him do what he wants. During the next election ... People are not so stupid. Let us have no fear.
I want to quote now an excerpt from the speech of the sponsor of the bill, who wanted to give us some indication of what IAC Limited is all about, and I quote:
I do not think it is necessary to explain at length the reasons for this bill, but I think it is necessary to outline some salient facts about IAC Limited. Since its founding in 1925, IAC has experienced an enviable growth record so that today it is Canada's eleventh largest financial institution,...
And we are proud of it as a financial institution-
. .. excluding insurance companies. It has more than 3,000 employees across Canada and over 12,000 shareholders, of whom more than 96 per cent are Canadians. The decision to seek legislation converting it into a chartered bank was made only after detailed study of how IAC could best continue to serve its customers, employees and shareholders in the rapidly changing Canadian financial system. The study concluded that IAC is at a competitive disadvantage by comparison with other financial institutions.
That is where I start wondering about some things, Mr. Speaker. I wonder how this company can be disadvantaged in its field as compared to other similar companies. If we compare it with banks, we are dealing with two different fields. I wonder why the hon. member said this company was disadvantaged as compared to other institutions. Hundreds of others will be disadvantaged so that it can join the bank monopoly. There is no competition going on, banks are not competing with each other. It's an absolute monopoly. And if this company is allowed to join the bank monopoly, are we not discriminating against hundreds of other companies that are in the banking business like IAC? It's a matter of justice, Mr. Speaker.
This is terrible in my opinion. In letters which I received from other very interesting companies, as able as IAC, I was told the following: Look at the discrimination involved if that bank is accepted. To be fair, you would have to accept 150 other ones. It has to be recalled that the main object of IAC is its former business which it has always carried out. I am not against IAC, but I want it to remain in its business. And I say there are enough chartered banks to control governments. Chartered banks are not even controlled by the Bank of Canada, they have free access instead to Canadian financial circles. And to think that a chartered bank which has only 4 per cent or 6 per cent of its reserve funds is entitled to multiply them by 16 per cent and to loan those funds at 12 or 13 per cent interest rates! It is a scandal throughout Canada, Mr. Speaker.

May 5, 1977
Continental Bank of Canada
It is scandalous. And they say that poor IAC should become a bank. It does not make enough money, it should take back its funds and multiply them by 16, not by 16 per cent, but by 16 to make even more money. This is our famous bank system. Let us give it the same as to all others. If we do it for one, we should do it for all others. I want justice. When we have given the same thing to all companies there will be enough of them for us to realize the ineptitude of our present system.
The hon. member continues as follows: We should note that almost 65 per cent of the present business of IAC is similar to that of chartered banks. Of course. It does not have the right to create credit like banks, that's all. It wants that right. IAC wants to create money from nothing, with $6 it wants to lend $100. This is the whole issue.
Over 90 per cent of IAC shares are of a kind that will allow the corporation to be assimilated to chartered banks if, as recommended in the white paper, banks are allowed to offer indirect services. IAC should become a chartered bank, whether the proposals made in the white paper are recognized or not. They do not care. They did say they could not care less until we get to the white paper proposals. Some people have interests in IAC and I am told that 90 or 95 per cent of shareholders are Canadians-I cannot find the place-96 per cent of shareholders are Canadians.
This is a monumental joke. They say that 96 per cent are Canadians but I would be interested to know the facts. The question has been put and it got a partial answer. One shareholder owns 19.6 per cent of the shares. If five shareholders own 51 per cent of the shares, they are not concerned about the others. They make people believe that the corporation is controlled by the people when in fact only four or five individuals direct the full operations of that finance company.
Well, I will oppose those moves as long as I live because at that rate we will end up with chartered banks completely outside the control of the Bank of Canada. What is forgotten today is that the Bank of Canada should be given the power it should have, that is the sole power to create currency, but instead of giving it that power they want to give it to chartered banks. The Bank of Canada alone should control monetary credit as legal tender, and then we would be in business.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to thank my colleague, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), for making a very specific statement on Bill C-1001.
Mr. Speaker, It will soon be five years that I first came to the House and I always ask myself a question that puzzles me, namely, why do such bills which favour finance or the setting

up of corporations to exploit Canadians, why do such bills seem to have seven lives? We keep killing them as they come but they always spring right back.
Yet, when we study a bill aimed at alleviating human suffering, at increasing old age pensions or family allowances, or at building roads or houses, there is always some government member to reject it. At five o'clock, they disappear.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the system in which we must work. Today we are asking this distinguished assembly at least to allow the establishment of a new bank. Are all of us who are here today sincerely convinced that the establishment of a new bank will improve the situation, reduce unemployment, put an end to the closing down of plants and stimulate business? I believe we now have in Canada ten chartered banks that are well organized and that can create all the necessary credit with a pencil and a piece of paper. There are 22 million people in Canada and we could all become overnight millionnaires because it is easy when we know where money comes from and how a dollar is made: you simply need a piece of paper and a pen to create credit.
My colleague said earlier that we had the right to create 16 per cent. It is not 16 per cent, but 16 times the amount on deposit. Chartered banks can create new credit. Our politicians have given them this privilege. We may well wonder why this privilege was extended to a group of individuals. However, it remains that this privilege was granted to a group of people who have a right of life or death on the development of our country. If those people control the air we breath, they would put it in storage and distribute it bit by bit, like they do for the monetary system.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I think there are enough chartered banks to meet our needs. Second, my colleague mentioned the Bank of Canada. This bank belongs to each Canadian. It was established by a good Liberal leader in 1934. At that time, he actually said that the Bank of Canada was designed to be a bank for all of us, to issue the funds required for the expansion and development of our country.
Unfortunately, that bank never served its purpose because someone came to our public men and said: Much good that will do you, but let me tell you this: when you need money, just come and see us and we will fix that, we will lend you money. It is not me who said it but someone opposite said that a people that does not control its economy, its currency, regardless of the laws it passes, is ineffective, and we have proof of this today. With all the banks we have, we are facing a terrible crisis, a record unemployment rate and we are unable to find answers to our problems.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote an internationally known economist, Mr. Paul A. Samuelson. He puts the following question: Do chartered banks really make or create money? I say yes and he also says yes. I should like now to quote some excerpts from his work. As I said earlier, we are now discussing banks and we must tell the people and members of the House that banks really create money and credit through the so-called process of multiple expansion of bank deposits. Most people have heard that by some mysterious conjuring tricks,
May 5, 1977

banks are able to make money. And, of course, without a single thing or rather with a piece of paper and a pen. However very few people realize how they go about it.
There is nothing really magical or obscure in the creation of bank deposits. It is obvious that anyone of us can deposit $100 or $200 in the bank with a deposit slip. This is wonderfully easy, there is nothing to it. Any intelligent person can easily follow the processing of the account, step by step. The real explanation of the creation of deposits is simple. The only hard things to understand are the false explanations which keep cropping up. Naturally, those who control the economic pulse of the nation have everything to gain by confusing things. According to these frivolous explanations, an ordinary bank manager could, with his pen, like I said earlier, loan out several dollars for each dollar in deposit.
It is no wonder then that experienced bankers see red when we infer they do likewise. They would like nothing better but they know well enough that a banker cannot invest sums or loan out money he simply does not have. Each dollar he uses to buy bonds or pay out a loan will eventually have to come out of his bank.
I have here certain examples of the banking system. That is why very often bankers go to the extreme opposite. They readily argue that the banking system as a whole is incapable of putting out money. So it is. Indeed, for the small change, the chicken feed that goes into our pockets, the Bank of Canada or the Canadian Mint must come into line. After all, banks can invest only the sums deposited by their clients. That is not true, it is totally false. They canot loan out the bank deposit. We create nothing, so they say, we are simply putting to work the community's savings.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that point is not valid. Bankers who suggest that fall victim to a fallacy we are all aware of but that still deserves refutation. What is true of one person may not be true of all. The banking system as a whole can accomplish what no individual bank can do, that is expand its loans and investments to the point where they become a multiple of the original volume of resources in the system, although in the process each small bank lends but a fraction of its deposits.
So we answer yes to the question put in the preamble to this section. Yes, the U.S. banking system and public taken together create some $5 in banking deposits for each dollar withdrawn from circulation to be deposited with the banks.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, obviously chartered banks have the privilege of creating credit.
Unfortunately, these credits have debts tied in. This is why it is said that there is a built-in debt in credit. A long lasting and sometimes bitter debt. We know that Canada is currently indebted to the tune of more than $54 million. Not so long ago, I read that the Jacques-Cartier bridge in Montreal and another bridge which was built in 1934 at the cost of $54 million, have been inaugurated. Having paid back $12 million already, we still owe $42 million on it. When shall we pay it off? God knows. And what will it lead us to?
Continental Bank of Canada
I do not know whether my great-great-grandchildren will ever finish paying it. When it is all paid up, the bridge will have long ceased being any good. And then, Mr. Speaker, they still have the nerve and cheek to ask for the creation of a new bank. One more bank or one less, that will not change the system but nevertheless, as my colleague said earlier, it would be a flagrant piece of injustice towards other finance companies which are dealing in the same business as IAC and as was said earlier, that would give them the chance to be part of a monopoly, a monopoly on the economic life of the nation.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker our good friends, from the New Democratic Party who are supposed to be a people's party so they say, a party working on behalf of small wage earners have finally given up. They thought that it was no use fighting anymore, and that it would take two more years before we could see any result. But within two years, a lot of things can happen. Besides, I think it is time to start fighting against this menace. If we wait another two years, things will get even worse. I wonder why the New Democrats let everything go. I remember last winter, when they were all enthusiastic. They would go around and say: We must prevent this from happening at any cost; but suddenly, nothing works anymore.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to question people's intentions, but as I said before, I am asking myself serious questions. I do not know what happened and I believe they had a flat tire on the way. That is why I wonder why we should not carry on in this party, not because of the IAC or of Mr. So and So, but for the good of each and every Canadian, as we have a very important part to play, in order to defend the interests of Canadians and of our children.
We are not alone. I am getting old, there are some younger than me here, but the fact remains that it is our sacred duty, Mr. Speaker, to take a position and uphold the rights of the people in this country. That is why we have agreed, not in a spirit of revenge, but merely to enlighten the people and make them aware, regardless of their religious beliefs and ethnic origins, of the direction in which our present system is leading us. It is leading us to bankruptcy, to hell, because we are in a vicious circle and there is only one way to get out of it.
As I mentioned earlier, we will never be able to pay completely for the Jacques-Cartier bridge and the Champlain bridge. Why? Because while paying for a bridge, we paid four or five others to financial institutions. The same is true in the present system of an individual who builds a home. He has every right to build a home. Everything is available. But we are told: To build a house, one needs money. No, money is not required. To build a house, Mr. Speaker, one needs lumber, nails, shingles, cement and workers, hammers and a saw. That is what is required to build a house. One does not say that a road cannot be built for lack of money. That is quite sensible. A bridge is not built over a river for lack of money. Quite sensible also. To build a bridge, Mr. Speaker, what does it take? It takes sand, cement, iron, engineers, and we have all that. It is quite ridiculous to be subjected to such a terrible system, because if you observe nature, you see that when bees

May 5, 1977
Continental Bank of Canada
want to build a nest, they do not ask anybody's permission. They find everything they need in their own environment and do not owe anybody anything. People say that money created out of nothing should be made available interest-free. The Bank of Canada should be responsible for that, for it would only mint-so to speak-our national resources. That is, why, Mr. Speaker, I shall keep on fighting as long as I live against the government granting another link to the credit monopoly, to high finance. I urge therefore all my followers to realize that we are fighting not against a phantasm, but against something real, our real enemies.
As I said, Mr Speaker, we do not object to this, but how is the bank supposed to finance investments or other financial assets it has acquired like any other buyer? It will, of course, make a cheque payable to its creditor or to the payee of a promissory note. If all these people agreed not to cash cheques at the bank or, which would come to the same thing, agreed to keep in a frozen account all the money received, the bank could then acquire all the assets it wished, without running the risk of losing a single cent of its cash flow. But nobody borrows funds at 6 per cent in order to leave them idle in a bank. The borrower uses them to process raw materials and produce, say, a car. The bank will therefore have to disburse, before long, the amounts equivalent to those loans. And if, as is likely, it is only one of the many financial institutions serving the town, the district, the state or the federation, it will recover only part of the amounts thus withdrawn.
The dispersal of the deposits in a bank which makes investments is further exemplified when it buys bonds or grants a loan to some local business. When a Boston bank buys government bonds, what are the chances that the bond dealer has an account with that bank? Such a probability is negligible. The dealer no doubt realizes that in New York, Los Angeles or Iowa, all the money is invested by the bank.
Mr. Speaker, naturally this may not be the time nor the place to go into the details or show proof of this national economic crime in Canada. It is neither the time nor the place, I think, to make you understand to what extent the gap widens each year between the income of the rich and that of the poor. And this in a very prosperous country known as Canada. And we who were entrusted by 23 million Canadians with the mission of restoring the balance through legislation and adequate figures, realize that we have sorrily failed in our mission. We realize that since 1967, when the Bank Act was revised, banks collect as much as 15 and 16 billion dollars in assets after taxes.

Mr. Speaker, when debating a subject such as this one we should be logical and sensible. Consequently, we should ask ourselves very appropriate questions. The objective of this bill being to have a charter for the creation of a new bank, it is therefore quite reasonable to ask oneself how much Canada or the Canadian people need a new bank now. Not so long ago, and it is still true today, we were ridiculed because we recommended economic measures which seemed revolutionary. We were used to hear again and again that our doctrine could be summed up in the printing of paper money and it was said that our objective was to issue paper money.
Mr. Speaker, I shall venture today to return the ball to those who would be in favour of a new bank. What do they want to do? What is the purpose of a bank? And particularly in this period of inflation when all Canadians are complaining about their low purchasing power, when prices are increasing so much that almost every week workers and even white collars are wondering how to make both ends meet because the prices of products and services are much higher than their purchasing power. However, if banks were trying to solve the problem of purchasing power, we could encourage them. But in the present economic system, banks are only deluding people.
We want to issue paper money but the banks only give illusions and utopias, for how could a new bank settle even an insignificant part of our economic problems? My colleagues insisted on that point. Of course, this is not the way to solve our problems. Consequently, the first thing we should ask ourselves when debating such a bill is whether we need a bank. It seems to me that this is only normal. But I tried to prove that we certainly do not need it for the moment. We are discussing the advisability of creating a bank when we are facing much more important problems. I am not aware of any bank problem in any area of the country, in any town and I would even say in any village.
There is certainly no shortage of banks. Even in the smallest localities, there is a tremendous competition between various banks, various financial institutions, whose purpose is to lend money. So there is absolutely no need for that, none at all. I would even say that such an initiative can only threaten to fuel the inflation which faces the country at the moment.
Mr. Speaker, we should certainly take advantage of the opportunity which will be offered us during the revision of the Bank Act, to find the means we could put at the disposal of all Canadians to try and seriously solve our economic problems. Of course, some people will say that by helping banks, which in turn make more credit available through loans, we could encourage investments which will lead to the progress we all wish. But, Mr. Speaker, we know very well that this is not what bank owners are after. Those are not the intentions of big financiers, and let me say briefly what those people really want.
May 5, 1977

Under the pretext of doing a service to Canadians, they want to incorporate banks with all the necessary branches. But I would say, Mr. Speaker, that people who are looking forward to creating new institutions want first of all to take advantage of loopholes in our financial and economic system to exploit, 1 repeat, to exploit Canadian citizens. They figured out that with such a system they could make money out of nothing. That is worse than the Social Credit money machine, Mr. Speaker, because those who want to create this new institution know full well that they need just a few million dollars in deposit to borrow 16 times this amount, as pointed out by my colleagues. Mr. Speaker, if it were not so hard and if I had the same intentions as those financiers, I could say: Let us get together and operate banks so that we can become rich.
But, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that our situation allows us to tolerate any further in this country any exploiters and exploited. I understand that regulations, laws and what have you allow us to do so, since we are fool enough to accept an economic system leading us directly towards a dead end. My colleague from Rimouski (Mr. Allard) very aptly explained that it was ridiculous, and I think we have to face it seriously.
I think it is about time we open our mind and our intelligence to the fact that finance, as it is managed, leads to an economic dead end. We are usually given as an excuse that this system is established throughout the world, that we have to follow it. But the example of the whole world is there to prove to us that it is a failure, because the problems of inflation and rising prices are problems which every country is facing and which seem in fact insolvable. This is a worldwide problem. That is why it is high time that a part of this world begins to think there is perhaps some way to change all this and drafts economic policies based for once on common sense and on the possibility for everybody to have access to the benefits of our economy, instead of having a small privileged group still taking advantage of the loopholes of the Bank of Canada Act and allowing these swindlers to take the money of Canadian taxpayers. In return for loans granted by the bank or those which are just based on fabricated credit, of course individuals, corporations, communities and even provincial governments borrow and pay back money which comes from our taxes. Mr. Speaker, some still do not understand today in 1977 that it is stupid, I would even say immoral, or at least amoral, to use the taxpayers' money to enrich high finance, and one cannot touch that, it is a dogma. Mr. Speaker, when will the representatives of the people understand that we are here to serve the people and not defend exploiters? Consequently, when it comes to taxes taken by the government out of the pockets of Canadian taxpayers that money must serve exclusively to initiate distributive justice, provide everyone with goods and services and not enrich a few individuals.
Mr. Speaker, when we still see today that pilgrimages have to be made to New York to feel the pulse of high finance, that is appalling. If we thought about it seriously I think we would be ashamed to see a country that is in a position to bring the United States to its knees to have natural gas, oil, paper and all kinds of valuable resources that abound here in Canada,

crawl to be able to get permission from American bankers. That is a crazy system, that is the right word, and for that reason it must be changed.
By accepting the institution of another bank when we do not have any shortage of those banks at home we are once again endorsing the principle of consecrating the system. And since we are opposed to the banking system as we have it in Canada you will understand that it is our duty to oppose as forcefully as we can a bill that seeks to institutionalize other banks in this country. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not be much longer on this matter. As I was saying before I called it five o'clock, it is not my intention, in raising this matter, to be critical of the Department of External Affairs or of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) or any of his officials. This is a difficult case, and I recognize that. The reason I am raising the matter is that, in order to reinforce the decisions of our court I believe there is an obligation on the government to go beyond the borders of Canada, wherever possible. The mother was in receipt of the decision rendered by the surrogate judge, Judge Fogarty, in Ottawa, which said in part:
Since Kazem-
Which is the name of the father
-and his daughter were strangers after the separation of more than six years, it was deemed unwise to send her to Iran.
In other words, the mother took guidance from the court in not allowing her daughter to go to Iran to visit her father, as had been allowed by a previous court at the time of separation when the custody of the child was given to the mother.

MayS, 1977
Judges Act
The other fundamental question that comes to mind is the matter of the rights of Canadian citizens. A Canadian citizen under the act has rights and obligations, and if the citizen abides by the laws and regulations of the country, surely the government should also abide by some of the obligations on behalf of the citizen. In this instance the young lady was kidnapped by her father, who subsequently left Canada.
Subsequently he came back to Canada, kidnapped his daughter in the true legal sense, and took her out of the country illegally. Her mother went to the RCMP, who said, "This is a family matter; we cannot act." At present the woman has no hope of regaining her daughter unless she goes to Iran, there to begin proceedings in court to regain her daughter. The mother is a Canadian citizen, without the resources which would enable her to go to Iran, pay for accommodation and hire a lawyer to work his way through the laws of a foreign country. She does not speak the language of that country. I therefore say there is an obligation on the federal government to represent the rights of this Canadian citizen in that country, and that is why I bring this matter forward this evening.
I greatly respect the Minister of Justice and think him a fair-minded, just person. I ask him to look into this matter, to see whether in the circumstances the Government of Canada can bring this matter before the courts of Iran, or have the young lady appear before some competent official there, to determine if she is happy or wants to return to her mother in Canada. She has said in many letters sent to her mother and grandparents, and in telephone conversations, that she wants to return.
Her mother is going through a most difficult time. Mr. Speaker, Vicki Starr, an 11-year-old citizen of Canada, was kidnapped from Canada against her will by her father, after he had been absent six years. Her father registered her citizenship and that of the mother in an embassy in Iran, by making a declaration without their knowledge or agreement. Yet a court in the province of Ontario had given custody of the child to the mother, who is a natural born Canadian citizen. Also, a court of the province of Ontario had advised the mother not to allow her daughter to go to Iran. In such circumstances, and one could mention other cases, I say the government is obligated to represent the rights of that Canadian citizen in a foreign court. If Canadian citizenship is to mean anything, the government must do it.
The distraught mother made representation to the Iranian embassy, and I think it is worth putting on record what happened. The Iranian ambassador reportedly said to Mrs. Starr, "At first it is natural for a mother who has lost her child to wail and gnash her teeth." He said that in time she will get over it. What sort of answer was that for a mother in such circumstances?
Although I am not a lawyer, I believe that the young lady's father attempted a form of blackmail. He said he wanted his daughter to come to Iran to visit him, but he laid down three

conditions. His former wife was to apply to a Canadian court, to have custody of the daughter transferred to him. He stipulated that the daughter must spend her entire summer holiday with him each year, and that the former wife should post a substantial cash bond in Iran to ensure that this condition was met promptly. He then demanded that all criminal charges outstanding against him in Canada should be withdrawn. That this should have happened I find incredible.
Writing to the mother, the young lady said, "I am fighting for my life. I am scared. Please help me." I talked to the mother this evening. She said, "We just can't get anywhere; it is maddening." She said, "I can't even go to Iran, to represent myself before the courts." According to two legal opinions, she is still an Iranian citizen, even though she is no longer married to the man, and, there is no guarantee that if she entered that country, she could ever leave it.
I have left this matter dormant for some time because our Department of External Affairs was trying to get the young lady back with quiet diplomacy. The mother was told that if somehow someone could spirit her daughter to the Canadian embassy in Teheran, since that embassy stands on Canadian soil the daughter would be safe and perhaps some way could be found to smuggle her aboard an aircraft and so return her to Canada. However, that is a hazardous way to reclaim your kidnapped child.
I shall rest the matter by pleading with the minister to look into this question carefully. If his officials wish to interview the mother, I shall be glad to make all necessary arrangements. The lawyer is in Ottawa but says his hands are tied. He can do no more. This unfortunate experience has been emotionally frustrating for the mother and her child. Mr. Speaker, the judgments of our courts must be upheld, enforced, and recognized by other countries. When they are not I say the Government of Canada is obliged to intervene on behalf of its citizens to make sure that justice is done in foreign countries.
I thank the minister and hon. members for hearing me. I know my comments were not strictly germane to the bill. Nevertheless, they relate to a family matter which has been before the courts. I hope that the few words I have spoken, together with the good offices of the Minister of Justice, will in small measure be instrumental in re-uniting this mother and daughter.

I also draw attention to salaries at the executive level of the public service. We saw a report from the so-called Lambert Committee-no relation to me-on executive salaries in connection with deputy ministers and senior grades in the public service. The newspaper columnists ran a 48-hour wonder in exclamation at the level of those salaries. The newspaper owners tut-tutted about it, without disclosing the fact that they were probably getting even more. But it makes the whole picture wrong.
When I was elected a member of parliament my salary was equivalent to that of a county court judge. But I find that according to this bill his salary will now go from $43,000 this year to $45,000, and next April it will go to $47,000.

speechtext:
Oh, the AIB, incidentally, rationalized the stupendous increase in judges' salaries of 1975

on the basis that provision had been made for it by statute prior to the invocation of the board. But so had the increase in the salaries of members of parliament. Then some weak-kneed individuals decided to run before the wind, and the result was that salaries of members of parliament were subject to the slash. But not those of judges. And those salaries have continued to rise to the extent that today they are far more than those of members of parliament.
Remember, too, that the expenses of judges are not controllable by the AIB while the expenses of members of parliament are. In somebody's twisted brain, the expenses are part of the compensation which is paid to members of parliament. But we face increases in the cost of hotels, automobile travel, and all the other items down the line. Businessmen face these increases but they get an adjustment in terms of their income tax. There is no question they can increase their expenses by 25 or 30 per cent on the basis of what they pay. Members of parliament face the same business expenditures in many constituencies, but there are some weak-kneed individuals who are afraid to stand up and say, "People who are in this business should be treated with an equal hand."
The judges, those who are on circuit, file their bills and they are paid. Provincial judges file their bills and they are paid. But not here. My participation tonight is only on this basis- that the government and the House must take their courage in their hands with regard to the treatment of executive salaries in the public service and elsewhere. Where there is a commission which makes a report, the government usually follows right along and the senior executives get those increases in salaries. Don't talk about expenses, because they get them too with no questions asked. Nobody talks about them, but they benefit by them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE TIME SPENT AS MAGISTRATE IN DETERMINING ELIGIBILITY FOR SENIOR POSITION
speechtext: Parliamentary secretaries and ministers benefit.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE TIME SPENT AS MAGISTRATE IN DETERMINING ELIGIBILITY FOR SENIOR POSITION
speechtext:
Why don't we in this country take the course followed in many another country? We know the difficulty. All the newspaper editors will say it is wrong for members of parliament to set their own salaries, that it is wrong for members of legislatures and members of city councils to do so. But, Mr. Speaker, who is going to set them? When I think of the newspaper publishers who complain about this in editorial columns it occurs to me that they have seats on the boards of directors of their newspapers and that, as directors, they set their own salaries. Directors of any corporation set their own remuneration, subject, it is true, to approval by the shareholders. But who has heard of shareholders objecting to it?
Oh, you will hear people complaining at the lower level that members of parliament should not be paid so much. But I invite them, first of all, to meet the general quality of members of this House. Two weeks ago I spoke about the contribution made by the backbenchers in this place, and after 20 years here I shall continue to fight for the right of the individual member of parliament who gets nothing but denigration. He
May 5, 1977

gets-I could use some awfully crude language but I am not in the league of the Prime Minister-very severely maligned.
The same can be said of all cabinet ministers as well as backbenchers; I do not differentiate between them in this connection. I know what the duties of a cabinet minister are and, quite frankly, the average cabinet minister is way underpaid the level of impost of income tax upon his salary. The same applies all through the legislatures. In countries like West Germany legislators at this level are paid more; their salaries are not taxed, and for a very practical reason. If they were, they would simply say that they had to increase their salaries in order to pay the tax. In France legislators are paid more than Canadian members of parliament. In the United States a Congressman's stipend has been increased to $57,000, and he has emoluments and allowances for staff which are not chargeable to him, as certain expenses do apply here in Canada.
I know many members of the House would like a global allowance for staff salaries which would depend on size of constituency and what have you. Members themselves would set the salaries of their staff, which would remove some of the obvious inequities which now exist. But no, Mr. Speaker, public opinion, spurred on by certain individuals and newspaper columnists, would say that the individual member of parliament is getting another $50,000, $60,000 or $70,000 a year. What balderdash! That is absolute and utter misrepresentation.
No public servant with a secretary-and some have several-is charged with the expense of his staff. No businessman is charged with the expense of his staff, and neither is a judge. And there are many judges, Mr. Speaker. I can see Your Honour is getting a little uncomfortable, but this affords the opportunity to me to make my general thesis, which is that there should be an independent statutory commission which, by law, would be charged to report back to parliament, either annually or every second year, on the level of compensation of senior public servants of the Government of Canada, members of the Parliament of Canada-including Senators-and members of the judiciary.
In this country we have the courts, the judiciary, on the one hand, and the administration, the public service, on the other hand. We also have the legislative arm, comprising ministers and members of parliament. In all logic and justice there must be some correlation at those levels if we are to call for top flight people in the public service. I am not averse to paying the man of demonstrated ability his just dues. I suppose that some people might accuse me of being an elitist; but only by looking at people who will set the highest standards of performance for themselves and who achieve those standards can we ultimately continue to strive for excellence. This applies not only to the public service but, as we all know, to business, although the rules of competition there are somewhat different. However, in the public service where merit is the ground rule we must certainly insist upon high standards.
Judges Act
I insist even more so, Mr. Speaker, that it be the rule in the courts that we have men of the highest quality going forward. And we will pay them well. A point where we certainly disagree is germane to this bill, and that is the question of extra high salaries for certain people in our society. This applies particularly in a time of restraint, at least a time when restraint is being preached to the general public and a time in which the little fellow is being asked to practise it.
I noticed this afternoon, when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) referred to the salary increases that are provided in this bill as only $2,000 a year, that he described them as modest increases. I suppose if your salary is in the $40,000 to $50,000 range that $2,000 is a modest increase. But I know a great many workers, a great many pensioners, and a great
May 5, 1977

many veterans who would love to have a modest increase of $2,000 a year. In this time, as I say, when the government is preaching restraint, I think it should be practised at the top.
I had not planned to make a speech along this line, but as I say, the views of my hard-working friend from Edmonton West prompted me to get to my feet again on this issue.
I believe that members of parliament, senior public servants, senior judges, football players, hockey players and a few others are getting too much. The fact that they are getting too much produces not only inequality but unhapiness and division in our society. I wish there were a little more of the practice of restraint at the upper level.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word in which I shall actually agree with the hon. member for Edmonton West, regarding the references made to the Anti-Inflation Board in the context of this bill. The Minister of Justice said that these increases of only $2,000 per year are below the $2,400 level and are therefore within the anti-inflation guidelines. Mr. Speaker, I am looking down this aisle to my friend, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). He and I, with others, sat with the Chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board a few months ago discussing the increase provided by statute for members of parliament, which was to take place in 1977. I am not now going to discuss whether there should have been any increase, as my views in that respect are well known, but I want to discuss it in relation to what has been put into this bill.
When we met with Mr. Pepin and other officials it was put on the table that, by statute, our taxable salary was supposed to have gone up by $1,600 and our tax-free allowance was supposed to have gone up by $700, a total of $2,300, or $100 below $2,400. It was thought that there was no problem, but we were reminded that an increase in salary produces an increase in contributions to the pension fund and other things of that nature.

My hon. friend, the minister, may reply in a moment. It was also drawn to our attention that whatever members of parliament might call our tax-free allowance, to the Anti-Inflation Board it was compensation. It interested me that the $100 was taken off the taxable portion and not the untaxable portion, but that is a reference on the side which I hope is understood.
I am not now discussing my views on high salaries among various groups. Those views are well known. It seems to me if those rules were made to apply to members of parliament and
Judges Act
members of the other place-if they were in particular made to apply to the Prime Minister and all other ministers as well as parliamentary secretaries, why should they not apply to judges? The $2,000 is less than $2,400, but they are on a pension scheme as well. A few years ago their pension was non-contributory but now it is contributory and the government matches it, and these other allowances, for travel, hospitality and so on, are being increased.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that when you put these things together they amount to precisely the same position as members of parliament were in; that the total increase in terms of the Anti-Inflation Board guidelines exceeds $2,400. It is not good enough just for the minister to say that he is satisfied that it is all right. I want him to tell the House whether the provisions of this bill were actually discussed with the Chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board and whether he gave answers to these questions comparable to the answers he gave to us when we discussed the position of members of parliament.
So, Mr. Speaker, I make that point. I intend to keep my remarks very brief. My colleague, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), has already indicated our general support of the bill. We think it should have second reading and go to committee. We also accept the proposition that there need to be more judges to do the jobs that have to be done in that field.

It is sometimes argued that they need it to write their judgments, but I thought they took time off between cases and wrote their judgments then. I put that question to the Minister of Justice.
Amongst items such as the Canadian Judiciary Committee and a few others there are, as I see it, two main things in the bill: one is an increase in pay, and the other an increase in the number of judges. I should like to ask the minister if he will tell us what discussions, if any, he had with Mr. Pepin about the increase in salaries and all the other perquisites and benefits. I should also like him to tell the House whether any consideration was given to increasing the length of the working year of judges as an alternative to adding to the number of judges provided in this bill.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE TIME SPENT AS MAGISTRATE IN DETERMINING ELIGIBILITY FOR SENIOR POSITION
speechtext:
It is not within the rules of this House that I have the opportunity to pronounce the benediction. I want to assure members of the House and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) that I do not want to carry

May 5, 1977
Judges Act
on so long that I will call it ten o'clock, either. I know that will warm the heart of my friends over there.
1 think this is a very important bill and it has given members an opportunity to express themselves with respect to a class of public servants in our community who, by the nature of their jobs, cannot express themselves with respect to a matter we can talk about freely, publicly, and openly. That is one of the privileges of belonging to parliament. 1 hope it is impressed upon people who read this debate that judges who are indeed privileged on the one hand with respect to the question of their tenure and in terms of their position in the community, have burdens upon them which none of us have, as well as restrictions in terms of their speech, movement, and association- even their right to express an opinion at the polls, something that .all of us have. All this puts the judiciary of Canada in a very unique position.
I am sure the Minister of Justice must be very pleased with the attention this House has given to the bill. I am sure he is equally pleased to know it is our intention to allow the bill to go to committee. It must be a very discouraging thing for a minister, whose departmental officials have laboured long and hard over a bill, to see it afforded only perfunctory debate in the House. I am sure the minister is pleased that it has received the attention it has in this House and to know that members of all parties will approve the principle of this bill.
I know of no greater responsibility a government has-there may be greater but I do not know of them-than choosing those men and women of the legal profession in Canada who will sit as judges in the courts over which the Minister of Justice and this government have jurisdiction. It casts a great responsibility upon the minister to make a recommendation to his colleagues, to canvass the opinion of the judiciary, canvass the opinion of the bar, and canvass the opinion of the community generally in the way it has to be done in respect of making appointments. This is important because once an appointment is made, a judge, except in very rare instances and circumstances, is then apart from the law of the normal society which all of us know very well. That is a very important consideration. That is what makes the office of the minister of justice one of the most important and why there has been a distinction by this Minister of Justice between his job as minister of justice on the one hand and as attorney general on the other. It is a very responsible ministerial position.
I must say that the system has been criticized from time to time by people who are uninformed about the canvassing that must go on if responsible appointments are to be made. Some say that it should be left to organizations such as the Canadian Bar Association, or a council of some kind, to make appointments, that the responsibility should be taken out of the hands of elected representatives and of the government, which has the majority in the House of Commons, and should be put somewhere else. I do not think so. I think the experience of the last few years-I say this about the minister himself in terms of his own appointments to the courts in this country and
[Mr. Baker (Grenville-Carleton).J
about his predecessors within my memory-has been that the appointments have been well made. The people who have been appointed have served well.
The bench in Canada, which is under the jurisdiction of the federal government, is a capable, discerning bench. The judges as a group are vested with a sense of concern, a good dash of horse sense and common sense, and the Minister of Justice and his predecessors in that important porfolio are to be commended for the quality of the appointments made to the bench.
One could not say that that is universal. There used to be a joke among lawyers that, "So and so is a very good judge, except for last week when he found against me; then I had second thoughts and reservations about him." But basically the quality of the bench has been very high and the minister and his predecessor deserve credit for that. I think it is important that appointments be made where the responsibility lies. That is not to say that this minister and other ministers and the government generally should not follow advice, or that responsible groups and people in the community should not solicit advice, because I think they should. But I do not think it would benefit our system if the appointment of judges as a matter of practice were taken out of the hands of the government, of the Minister of Justice and his cabinet colleagues. I think that kind of appointment should not be handed to any organization which might be deemed to be a clique of some kind and not responsible.
It has also been said that it is important that judges-if you are speaking about male judges-be gentlemen in their conduct, and if you are speaking about women, that they be the female alternative of gentlemen, in the sense that with respect to those who appear before them as counsel and those who appear before them as litigants or as accused, that they show a reasonable amount of compassion and concern and a sense of common decency. I think most of them show it. I think it is perhaps even more important than a high academic knowledge and a great deal of learning with respect to the law.
Lawyers in courts who are properly instructed can and do help a judge in his work. If a judge happens to have a fair knowledge of the law, that is a bonus in terms of his appointment. But I think that basically his human qualities are more important in the long run than his qualities of legal learning, which can be acquired.
I think it is important also that in considering candidates for the bench, whether men or women, that those candidates not be appointed too early in life. Experience at the bar is a great leveller. Experience in the practice of law brings a lawyer into contact with all kinds of cases, all kinds of human beings, and it develops knowledge and a sense of understanding, which are important. Perhaps it also develops a sense of tolerance in terms of human behaviour which helps a judge understand the complexities of the law. There is nothing like experience in that way.
It is also salutary in another way that people sometimes do not talk about. I think it is important, aside from all the things that I have mentioned, that judges not be appointed too early in their lives because the appointment has such permanency to
May 5, 1977

it. If by chance a judge does not adjust himself to the bench and cannot adjust himself to the structures of that life and finds that he does not enjoy it, his conduct in the courtroom as part of the judicial process is affected thereby and perhaps he will not make the best judge or the best human being in that job. This is the reason why the question of judges' salaries becomes important because, whether we like it or not-and if I were practising I would like it-the fact is that legal incomes in Canada have risen to a great degree and if a man or woman is being considered for appointment to the bench at the age of 45, 50 or 53-in that age range, which is not a bad age, I respectfully suggest, to appoint a judge-he or she must consider giving up that way of life at the height of their earning power and the height of their abilities. This does create problems.
Judges, lawyers, and accountants are no different from anyone else. Each has a certain standard that he sets for himself, each has a certain obligation to his family, some heavier than others. If it is the object of this bill-and I think it is at least in part-to ensure that the level of the salary will not be an enticement to the bench on the one hand and, on the other hand, will not be a deterrent to the bench, then the principle of the bill in that sense is supportable. For that reason I go along with the minister with respect to the bill.
The other aspect of the bill is the amount of work with which judges and the courts are faced. I do not think there is anyone who has ever practised in any court in any province of this country before judges who have been appointed by the Minister of Justice, who will ever say that they can go to a client and say to him that his business is being processed quickly, and not blush a little. Some of that blushing is earned in the sense that from time to time lawyers, like everyone else in any profession or business, tend to get themselves too involved. Some of it is not earned by the profession. Actually a lot of it is not. Some of it is earned by the sheer burden placed on courts because of new causes of action created by new technology.
As the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) mentioned, a disproportionate amount of the time of our county court and superior court judges in Canada is taken up with motor vehicle litigation, and if justice delayed is justice denied, we can place a great part of the blame on motor vehicle litigation which has slowed the wheels of justice. Rights must be adjudicated upon. The question falls within the purview of this government and it must be considered. Also, the legal profession, governments and the bench will have to decide quickly how this matter is to be dealt with.

speechtext:
The question is being considered carefully.
The other aspect of my remarks concerns the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who spoke a few minutes ago about lengthening the working
Judges Act
year of Her Majesty's judges. I have the greatest respect for the hon. member. He is my friend and neighbour, a former printer, and a learned fellow, who goes around this House rapier in one hand and Standing Orders in the other. I say to him, in friendship, that it is not just a question of lengthening the working year of the courts.
I think a good case could be made for changing the arrangements under which our courts work. My own view is that a good case could be made for joining together into one court the superior court and county and district courts of the province of Ontario, and their equivalents in other provinces. I would include in this arrangement the trial division of the Ontario Supreme Court. All these courts I would make into one court. There is a good case to be made in support of that idea. That case is being strengthened because our county judges are assuming ever more duties; yet, as I recall, their salaries are somewhat lower than those of high court judges. I suggest that this fact alone strengthens the case for amalgamation.
There is also a good case to be made for decentralization of our courts. A good case could be made in this province, Ontario, as well as in other provinces, for establishing districts which would come under the jurisdiction of the amalgamated courts. Perhaps we could appoint even more judges, who could do their work in a smaller area. Mr. Speaker, it is hard for a judge to travel around a province, although some judges like to travel. At present our supreme court judges in Ontario must travel around the province a good deal. But that disrupts their family life and creates a whole series of difficulties. I do not think travelling necessarily advances the efficiency of our administration of justice, and we could well consider decentralizing our courts and dividing the province or provinces, into administrative areas. As I say, a good case could be made for joining together into one court our county, district and superior courts, in which I include the trial division of our supreme courts.
It may be difficult to convince the public, who are the final judges, that it is absolutely necessary for all superior courts of this country to close down during the summer months. I am speaking of closing in an operational sense. One could with imagination devise methods whereby judges could stagger their holidays and periods when not on the bench. It makes good sense for judges to have time away from the bench, for they need time to write their reserve judgments. Let me put it this way. It would be difficult to convince me that there is a case to be made for continuing the operation of our superior courts all through the summer months.
Perhaps hon. members will recall that a former member of this House, a Privy Councillor, Hon. Richard Bell, served as a member of the Ontario Law Reform Commission. He presented a minority report. I point out that the commission in part reviewed the province of Ontario court system. I commend a reading of that minority report on the organization of the courts to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and to those interested in the administration of justice. That minority report of course was not accepted, but it brought to the
5342

May 5, 1977
Judges Act
attention of the public, the legislators and people of Ontario, an alternative to the present system.
The public is questioning the present system. It suffers from delays, some of which are created, I suppose, by the very nature of the system; others of which are created in part by the nature of the profession. It is important to keep these matters under review. Since passage of this bill will ease the load on judges, it is worthy of support on that second ground.
I look forward to the day when we shall have a unified family court system. All the matters with which our courts deal come under the law, and I do not know of any aspect with which our courts deal which is outside the law. However, I think matters pertaining to family law really have no place within the adversary system; I think they are out of place in an adversary system, just as the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) is out of place sitting next to the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme). I hope the Minister of Justice will do his best within the purview of his authority to urge the matter of unification in the context in which I have raised it, since such an important initiative would have general support in the community at large. I suggest it would have the support of the profession in general, including that of the bench.
I welcome the appointment of women to the bench. Although no self-respecting female member of the bar would suggest that women should be appointed in accordance with a quota, no one would argue that women are not as capable as men in matters pertaining to the law. Indeed their sense of compassion is at least equal to, if not greater than that of men, and they are just as capable as men in handing down judgments. I therefore think that the minister's efforts to appoint women to the bench are worthy of support.
Finally, I raise the question of court facilities. I suggest that the federal government and the profession should consider the adequacy of our court facilities in the province of Ontario and other provinces. Mr. Speaker, I have pleaded in many court houses. Many are fine, old, historic buildings which deserve to be preserved, if possible. However, in terms of facilities, many of them are very unsatisfactory. I am afraid to say that facilities in the provincial courts of Ottawa and the national capital region are so poor as to bring the administration of justice into disrepute. I hope it will not be lost upon those in authority, and I am sure it will not be, that court facilities in this city must be improved.
It is difficult to imagine, but on one occasion in the provincial court in Ottawa, a trial was held before a provincial court judge in a room in one of the Holiday Inns in this city. Instead of the flag being the flag that is to the right of you, Mr. Speaker, the flag happened to be the house flag of Holiday Inns. There was no picture of the sovereign who is the head of state. It was not missing for any perverse reason, but simply because there was not one available. That was a criminal court, a court before which a citizen is brought, and presumed to be innocent until proven guilty. It is a court where the

public come as witnesses and where a judge sits. I believe these deplorable conditions are repeated in many parts of Canada.
I recognize that this is not the direct responsibility of the Minister of Justice. However, if the time comes when we are negotiating or considering the restructuring of the court system of this province, I hope the minister will not feel so out of it that he will not advance the proposition that he who appoints the judges has some obligation to be concerned about the facilities in which they must play their part in the administration of justice.
In closing, I commend the minister for bringing forward this bill. We are very pleased to'accommodate him in terms of bringing the debate to a conclusion with respect to second reading. I am sure the minister is pleased that the profession and the courts have received the attention of this House that they deserve, and that the passage of this bill and its movement to committee do not take place only after perfunctory attention. It is important that we never lose sight of that one group of people who, by their nature, cannot speak for themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE TIME SPENT AS MAGISTRATE IN DETERMINING ELIGIBILITY FOR SENIOR POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in order that other business of the House can proceed. I want to express my appreciation to hon. members who have spoken on the bill and my appreciation of their willingness to allow it to move into the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for clause by clause discussion.
I want to comment on a few points made by some of the speakers during the course of the debate, particularly the critic of the official opposition, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). He offered a very constructive group of comments on the bill.
The hon. member raised the issue of the unified family courts and why I was not able at this point to have some firm agreement with all of the provinces as to the number of unified family court judges that would need to be appointed over the next few years. The simple answer to that is that we are developing these on an experimental or pilot project basis. At this point it is impossible to determine how quickly provincial attorneys general or their legislatures will move in the formation of unified family courts.
We have the agreements I specified in my speech, one with Ontario to commence operation on July 1, an agreement in principle with Newfoundland, one with Manitoba to start on July 1, and other provinces that I mentioned in my speech. However, it is impossible at this point to specify in legislation how many judges will be required. It is for this precise reason that we have adopted in clause 18 the flexible approach of having a reserve pool from which we could appoint judges, either of the superior court or district court, to be judges of unified family courts as they are established by the provinces.
May 5, 1977

The other option would be not to make this provision and to enter into agreements with provinces to form these courts. Each time they did, we would have to come back to parliament to amend this act in order to create a position to fill it.
I think the hon. member for Calgary North was supportive of the clause. I just give him that explanation as to why at this point we are unable to give the precise number of judges that are needed. My own hope would be that we would need all of them and that we would use up that reserve pool as quickly as possible. Obviously the whole thrust of my interventions and discussions with provincial attorneys general over the past 18 months has been to encourage them to form unified family courts.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) raised a number of interesting points. One was the question of merger. He raised the issue that the public is often confused as between superior courts and district courts or county courts, and that maybe the time has come to merge them. Of course they have been merged in Prince Edward Island and Quebec for a long period of time.
Whether the two levels of courts are merged or not is a decision for provincial attorneys general and provincial legislatures. I want to be very clear in this to the hon. member for Broadview. I have made it unequivocally clear to provincial attorneys general who, after all, are in charge of the administration of justice and have constitutional responsibility therefor, that if they and their governments make the decision that the courts in their province should be merged, they will have no opposition whatsoever from me and I will forthwith introduce the necessary legislation to bring that about.
I would point out that it is essentially a provincial decision that must be made as to what is the best system for the administration of justice within a particular province. As I say, I have indicated to them that I have no philosophic, political or governmental objection to that step being taken. I will anticipate that possibly over the next year or so we will see in some of the provinces mergers of the two levels of courts taking place.
The only concern that I might have, and that I have expressed, is that in any merger proposals, provision be made for adequate judicial service throughout the whole of the province either by circuits, rota or changes of residence of the judges. That is really the only observation that I have.
The subject is one of heated debate in some provinces, heated in respects that I think are unnecessary and unwise. Often it seems to turn on the question of personalities, of either the superior court judge looking at the district court judges and saying they do not want to serve together, or the bar looking at a certain person and saying that he should or should not be a judge. That should really not be the basis upon which either chief justices or chief judges or attorneys general or presidents of bar associations make a decision or a representation upon the question.
Judges Act
The hon. member for Broadview also raised the question of discipline through the Judicial Council. The Judicial Council, as set up under the Judges Act in sections 30, 31 and 32, has functions which include education, and the pursuit of judicial uniformity, all of which it does very well. It also serves as a disciplinary body for judges appointed by the governor in council. It may, at the request of myself or of a provincial attorney general or on its own initiative, institute an inquiry or an investigation into the conduct of a judge. It is, I find, an immensely worthwhile institution to have.
In the old days the only way to deal with a judge against whom there might be a serious complaint, either valid or invalid, was through a representation to the Minister of Justice who was then placed in a truly impossible position. He had what might be a valid complaint on his desk. On the other hand, as a member of the executive, he could not interfere with the conduct of judges. I think it was one of my predecessors as minister of justice, the hon. Mr. Garson, who said he never figured out how to deal with these complaints in what he regarded as a satisfactory manner.
Nowadays, if there is a complaint made to me it is forwarded automatically to the Judicial Council. Often it happens that people write directly to the Judicial Council. Complaints range from those of unsuccessful litigants who are unhappy with judges because of court decisions, to serious allegations which are dealt with seriously by the Council. The ultimate remedy under the act is the removal of a judge on the recommendation of the Council; at that point I bring the recommendation before parliament for the appropriate action under the British North America Act. I might add that this has never happened since the Judicial Council was established.
The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) discussed a number of matters, including discipline. He mentioned, as did the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), the question of court facilities. The latter comes from one of the richest provinces in Canada, and the other hon. member comes from one of the least rich. I would point out, however, that the administration of justice, which includes the provision of appropriate court facilities, is a provincial responsibility and that any interference from me or the federal level in this regard would be strongly resisted.
I might tell the hon. member for St. John's West that I have inspected some of the facilities in St. John's. Indeed I have gone over the courthouse from the belfry to the basement and discussed the matter with the attorney general, Mr. Hickman. I would also point out to the hon. member that the payment made to Newfoundland in equalization grants amounts to some $234 million a year and that the whole purpose of equalization is to allow the less rich provinces to provide public services of the necessary national standard. I think it would be most unwise to enter into cost-sharing schemes in every line of activity or in connection with every provincial program. Assistance in these areas is precisely the purpose of equalization. It is up to Newfoundland or to any other province to decide what

Judges Act
its priorities shall be and how best to expend the money received.
The hon. member also discussed the Doyle case. I take serious exception to what he said. I have examined the matter and I have stated in this House that there is no negligence on the part of any minister or on the part of any of the officials involved. Having said that once, 1 would expect the hon. member to accept my statement instead of continually attacking it and challenging it as he does.
Second, I wish that when he was attacking me this afternoon-I notice he is not in the House this evening-he had read into the record my complete answer the other day: that there is one case before the Supreme Court concerning which an adjournment has been agreed to which will result in a delay of four or five months, and that the particular case to which he referred, which has been filed for appeal in the Supreme Court of Canada for seven years, has not been proceeded with for technical legal reasons, on the advice of the law officers of the Crown that it would be unwise to proceed with that appeal until another case has been settled in a federal court relating to the same assessment. I rather resent this being characterized as an improper or negligent way of conducting the case. I say from my place in the House of Commons that the law officers of the Crown have been instructed to proceed with all these cases as expeditiously as the law and the rules of the court allow. I would ask that the hon. member read this statement and accept it in accordance with the practice of this House.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) raised a number of issues, including the appointment and the method of appointment of judges. The hon. member for Calgary North, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, and the hon. member for Broadview all discussed appointments and I think they approached the subject with the proper judicial and judicious attitude. But the hon. member for Edmonton West launched into something of a tirade about political appointments. I thought, first, that he was preaching for a call. It turned out that he was preaching for a pay increase. Being an elder statesman-one with more hair than I but still an elder statesman-he may be a little out of touch, as is common among some elder statesmen. May I, on the appointment question, read to him from one of a series of lectures in 1975-76 collected under the title of "The Canadian Judiciary", published by the Osgoode Hall Law School and edited by Mr. A. M. Linden. I read from a commentary on judicial appointments by William H. Angus, Professor of Law at Osgoode Hall:
One can only applaud the favourable developments over the past ten years in the method of judicial appointment by the federal government. These achievements are all the more remarkable when viewed in the context of a century of dissatisfaction with the exercise of the appointing power since Confederation. Our guest lecturer has very ably described the recent events with clarity and frankness.
His own substantial contribution to the process should not be overlooked when acknowledging the credit due to three previous Ministers of Justice and the present incumbent-
[Mr. Basford.J
The present incumbent being myself.
-who is publicly committed to continuing the policies of his immediate predecessors.
My first comment on the lecture is directed to the future. Although the old ad hoc approach to judicial appointments has been replaced by a "system", to use the language of our guest lecturer, the new order is still an impermanent structure as presently constituted. The true test will come with a change of government, which is bound to occur sooner or later.

Hold your applause for a moment.
After the first flush of that electoral victory will come a perhaps understandable, although regrettable in my opinion, desire to reward party supporters. Whether this motivation can be resisted in the sphere of judicial appointments to preserve the advances achieved since 1967 is problematical at this point in time.
Having listened to the hon. member for Edmonton West, I suggest it is not only problematical but certain. He spoke of the judicial process and said, apparently, that it was wrong because there was not a minister from Edmonton at the particular time of which he spoke. He indicated to me very clearly that he could not wait to get into office to return to the pre-1967 days. At no point in his speech about the judicial appointment process, regarding which he criticized me and my predecessors, did he put in place or suggest any system. He seemed to be totally unaware of the present system which is commented on in this series of lectures which I have quoted; and he certainly indicated to me that Professor Angus is indeed right when he says that he has some fear of what might happen to the judicial appointment process if ever there were a change in government.
I make one last point in relation to the comments made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The compensation allowances provided for in this bill were discussed not by me but by my officials with the officials and members of the Anti-Inflation Board, and I am advised that they have been approved as being within the guidelines. The increase is $2,000 in dollar terms and $400 to take account of other items of compensation, including pensions. As I say, they have been examined by the officials of the AIB and are deemed to be within the guidelines.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre also raised the question of the work of judges, and this was picked up by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton. I touched upon a few of those questions in my speech this afternoon in regard to the work judges are doing in terms of judicial education, the experiments they are conducting in pre-trial procedures and in speeding up the process. However, I am delighted that the hon. member raised the subject again because I think it is one to which judges from one end of the country to the other have to pay careful attention. This able and dedicated group of people are in fact organizing their affairs and their case loads in as efficient a way as possible.
