subtopic: TRADE-GATT NEGOTIATIONS-REQUEST THAT CANADA NOT TAKE POSITION ENDANGERING EMPLOYMENT
TRADE-GATT NEGOTIATIONS-REQUEST THAT CANADA NOT TAKE POSITION ENDANGERING EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity of pursuing this evening my attempts to obtain more information about the approach of the Canadian delegation at the current round of negotiations relating to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and also to obtain assurances that Canada's goal at these negotiations will be to safeguard Canadian jobs, especially in the manufacturing industry and particularly the automotive parts and electrical industries.
The world is experiencing a difficult economic situation, plagued by increased production costs and the prospect of shortages of energy and other resources. Since the Toyko declaration on GATT in 1973, political instability, economic recession, inflation, and the oil crisis in particular are contributing to a decrease in the chances of achieving the goal of greater trade liberalization. Spokesmen for Canadian manufacturing industries have expressed concern about the present state of their competitiveness and the future of Canadian jobs, especially when faced with increasing domestic and economic
Adjournment Debate
problems and the present difficult position of Canada at the negotiating table in Geneva.
The current economic climate appears to be inhospitable to Canada's chances of obtaining easier access to foreign markets. Unless Canadian negotiators are successful in this goal, the Canadian manufacturing industry will suffer, jobs will be lost, and our standard of living will fall. It is therefore vital for us that the federal government be most prudent and very skilful so that our men in Geneva may extract the best deal. In addition, our government here at home must develop new and rational industrial strategies without further delay.
Although Canada is a large trading nation, our balance of trade has been deteriorating. We have been for too long exporters of raw materials, and heavy importers of manufactured goods. In 1976 we imported $23 billion worth of these goods and ended last year with a deficit in the balance of trade in manufactured goods totalling $10 billion, which is higher than any other country in the world. This reveals a lot about our lifestyle, the openness of the Canadian market, and the precarious competitive position of manufacturing industry in Canada. The realities of international trade and the Canadian economic environment are such that Canadian manufacturing industries have to compete against the combined efforts of foreign manufacturers and the industrial strategies and trade policies of their governments.
The negotiating strategies of those countries in Geneva are based upon the industrial strategies of those countries. Moreover, those industrial strategies reflect the philosophy that a strong domestic base for industry is a necessary prerequisite to competitive exports. However, in Canada we do not have yet an articulated equivalent rational industrial strategy and a favourable economic environment that would give our industry a fighting chance to compete in the international market.
It is this predicament and the prospect of facing a 50 per cent reduction in tariffs that are producing great apprehension in certain manufacturing industries and among their employees. It is understandable, therefore, that they are reluctant to see our government make concessions that will greatly encourage imports from other countries. Furthermore, too many concessions made by Canada at Geneva could further aggravate the employment situation in our manufacturing industries, especially in the electrical and automotive parts. That is why we hope Canada will be successful in pressing for the elimination of the non-tariff barriers and also will firmly insist on the sectoral approach to the GATT negotiations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRADE-GATT NEGOTIATIONS-REQUEST THAT CANADA NOT TAKE POSITION ENDANGERING EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) recognizes the great importance of the automotive industry to the economy of Canada, and the electronic portion of that as well. The minister also recognizes the contribution continually made by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) to the interests of this industry. It should be able to survive and indeed prosper.

May 5, 1977
Adjournment Debate
We all know the automotive industry, generally, was the one sector of our economy which provided the greatest share of deficit in our international trade in the last year. However, with respect to the GATT negotiations and the ongoing negotiations there, a successful negotiation which leads to a substantial reduction of foreign barriers to trade will create important new opportunities for Canadian exports. Equally important, a carefully managed and sensibly staged reduction of Canadian trade barriers, accompanied by appropriate domestic measures including, where necessary, assistance from government, will help in achieving the structural changes needed to make the Canadian economy more efficient, more competitive, and more capable of meeting inflationary pressures.
This is the seventh round of negotiations since GATT was signed in 1947 and marks the first time that there is a systematic effort to negotiate on both tariffs and non-tariff barriers to trade, whether applicable to agricultural or industrial products. All our major trading partners are engaged in these negotiations. Just as we will be seeking major benefits for our exporters, we will be expected to contribute our share of concessions. At the same time, the government has clearly demonstrated its willingness to act expeditiously in instances where rapid and unprecedented growth in imports creates short term, emergency situations. Examples include recent measures on clothing and certain other textile imports where rapid increases were putting at serious risk employment in those industries.
The government is conscious of the need to maintain a close and continuing dialogue with the private sector on the current negotiations. To this end the Canadian trade and Tariffs Committee has received over 250 submissions from the private sector outlining particular views and concerns about the negotiations, including those of the automotive and other secondary manufacturing industries. Through this process, which includes formal meetings with firms, associations and interests representing all sectors of the Canadian economy and all regions of the country, account is taken of the views expressed by the private sector as the necessary Canadian negotiating positions are developed. Through the activities of the Parts Manufacturers' Association and their very able representative, Mr. Pat Laval, its views are being pressed upon the minister daily.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-LEVEL OF INFLATION BY END OF YEAR-RESTRAINT ON SPENDING BY ALL LEVELS OF GOVERNMENT
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-LEVEL OF INFLATION BY END OF YEAR-RESTRAINT ON SPENDING BY ALL LEVELS OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 111 asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) a question which was basically to inquire if he was still confident that we will achieve a 6 per cent inflation level by the end of the year. The minister replied in part as follows:
If we can maintain additional restraint and achieve a further reduction on the non-food price side, then indeed the target can be attained.
{Mr. Poulin.]
On May 3 the minister changed his tune when he replied to a question put by my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) in part as follows:
... it might be a difficult target to meet. I hope we will not reach the 7 per cent level, but this will depend on events through the year.
A further question was put by me dealing with the minister's fiscal and monetary policies. I asked the minister when we would hear from the government as to when it proposes to terminate wage and price controls. The minister said he would make a statement in that regard in the budget context. The budget has come and gone and still no termination date has been suggested for the controls or anti-inflation program. We have had no indication as to what would be the new contingency plan in view of the fact that the anti-inflation program is not working. In fact, if it were not for our energy and resource wealth we would have one of the worst economic records of any of the main industrialized nations at the present time.
Let us look at the record in Canada compared to that of the United States, our main trading partner. In 1975 our real growth was 4.8 per cent compared to 6.2 per cent in the United States. Our consumer prices went up 7.8 per cent last year compared to 5.8 per cent in the United States which has no controls. We had more people out of work in this country than any other large industrialized nation.
Our current account balance was $4.9 billion in deficit last year as it was the year before, compared to the United States which in those two years was in surplus. Even the United Kingdom had a deficit less than ours in the past two years. Most alarming, hourly compensation in manufacturing jumped 12.9 per cent last year compared to 7.3 per cent in the United States. That means we are continuing to lose our competitive position with the United States.
In Canada we paid our workers in manufacturing last year $7.39 while the United States paid $6.90-yet we had controls and of course the U.S. did not. That is a difference of 49 cents per hour. The year before, 1975, there was a difference of only 9 cents per hour, and of course in 1970 the rate in the United States was $4.20 and we were at a level of $3.46. We were 74 cents below the average rate in the United States; now we are 49 cents above the United States wage level in manufacturing.
I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that that is after the government's so-called anti-inflation program which has been in position since mid-October 1975.
Just let me cite a few more Figures. For example, in textiles our workers are now paid $5.30 compared to the United States where they are paid $4.55; in footwear our level is $4.55, and the United States level is $4.10. I could go through various other sectors of our economy. I am suggesting that this is an important reason why we now have the worst of all worlds- high inflation and high unemployment. Trends in productivity spell this fact out. For example, in the United States last year productivity went up 8.4 per cent while ours went up 3.5 per cent. This is one of the worst increases of any industrialized nation.
In unit labour costs and manufacturing our record is absolutely deplorable. Last year these costs jumped 11.7 per cent
May 5, 1977

while in the United States they actually went down 1.9 per cent.
In short, Mr. Speaker, the government has got to start coming clean with this House. It has to start giving answers on why inflation is rising notwithstanding its so-called anti-inflation program. It has to show why we are in such a stagnant position compared to our main trading partner, the United States, and it has to show what its new contingency plan to stop inflation in this country Js going to be. Clearly the program it outlined in 1975 is not working but we cannot get from it today any indication of when it plans to terminate the wage and price control program. We can get no indication as to whether it plans to use more or less fiscal restraint, more or less monetary restraint, but we have these figures piling up month by month showing that our economy is in a very serious condition.
Typically, this government rather than re-evaluate its own shortsighted policies has chosen instead merely to revise its goals. What else can you read into the comment made by the minister last Tuesday when he was asked a straight question as to whether we were going to achieve a 6 per cent goal, and he said, no, but he hoped that the new target of 7 per cent would not be achieved? In short, the policy of ministers opposite seems to be: if at first you do not succeed, lower your sights. It is time the country was rid of them.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-POTENTIAL DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA- SUGGESTED DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON JOINT ACTION
AGRICULTURE-POTENTIAL DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA- SUGGESTED DISCUSSIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON JOINT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my reference in the adjournment debate is last March 9, as recorded at page 3798 of Hansard. That was the occasion when the issue of the serious drought in western Canada was first raised in the House in a series of questions by my leader and by myself addressed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). Hon. members may remember that that was the first time that the critical drought situation was mentioned in parliament. It has been raised many times since, including today's question period when by coincidence my questions to the same minister were essentially on the same subject, namely, the drought in Canada.
I am sure hon. members will recall that on the first occasion on March 9 the minister's response to our plea for immediate emergency action was to ask all members of the House to pray for rain. I am sure all of us who fully appreciated the extent of the drought crisis did indeed pray for rain, and are not ashamed to say so. This was the same minister who, two and a half weeks later, according to a feature article carried in the Canadian Week End magazine, said in a speech he delivered at Tilley, Alberta, that the free market system is as outdated as Jesus Christ, and almost as redundant.
Last March 9 the minister was more than a little uneasy and touchy about my drought questions, and he was equally uneasy and touchy today when I raised the same subject. His completely evasive answers on those occasions were exceedingly disappointing to me, as they were, I am sure, to every farmer in the extensive drought belt of the west. Surely the Minister of Agriculture knows that this serious drought is a non-partisan, non-political issue. It is much too serious to make quips about or to joke about, and one cannot assume credit for the first rain of any consequence to fall in over nine months. Mr. Speaker, the first significant amounts of rain fell last night and today on most of the western Prairies.

May 5, 1977
Adjournment Debate
I asked the minister last March, and again today, about a joint emergency drought approach involving the prairie provincial governments, and about a sharing of information with the United States. I understand there have been no such meetings with the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan. If they have taken place, let the minister say so and put out a positive press release. Why be so secretive? Western farmers are aware of the concern, and of the quick response and action taken by United States federal government agencies with respect to their vast drought areas.
On Tuesday of this week the government of Alberta announced a crash program for deep water well drilling and the companion to it, a program for pumping and pipelining water for both stock water and small town domestic use. I ask the minister again, now, will the federal government enter into a cost-sharing arrangement with Alberta and the other Prairie provinces on this and other emergency programs? Failure to act now, or at least to give a firm indication of federal action, will only contribute to a further degree of disaster in the west.
Almost all related agricultural industries and most service industries are hurting badly today in western Canada, Farm machinery sales are down between 30 per cent and 45 per cent from levels of one year ago. Receipts at Prairie stockyards have jumped in the last three weeks or more by as much as 40 per cent, and in southeast Alberta, by 50 per cent. It is now inevitable that the Prairie cattle industry will suffer more than the grain industry, and a continued drought could lead to a drastic reduction in western cattle poulations, at the very time markets and prices are definitely on the upturn.
The drought situation demands co-operation and action by the three principals involved. Farmers, especially cattle producers, have already made significant sacrifices by drastically reducing their herd numbers to fit their grass and feed supplies. At least some provincial governments have already acted. Is it too much to ask for leadership and immediate action from our federal government now?
In closing, I thank the Minister of Agriculture for attending in the House this evening. Perhaps the minister could use his influence with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Les-sard) to open immediately the Suffield PFRA pasture for use this year.

Mr. Speaker, let me comment first on what the hon. member said about praying for rain. I was quite serious when I told the House of Commons that I hoped our people would pray for rain. The hon. member's leader said at the time, "Is that all that the Minister of Agriculture has to offer the farmers of western Canada, prayer and fertilizer?" Yesterday the hon. member's
former leader, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), after hearing the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion reply to his supplementary question, as reported on page 5275 of Hansard, said:
Mr. Speaker... I would ask him whether the original plan suggested by the Minister of Agriculture, that he was going to pray for rain, has been departed from?
It has rained recently in western Canada, Mr. Speaker. Of course, all the meetings of our agriculture, DREE and environment officials did not bring on the rain, but I think it is in order to say a prayer of thanks for the rain we received.
The hon. member referred to some comments of mine, as reported in a Canadian magazine. I think I was reported by a newspaper yesterday as saying that when I saw the article I knew I would be in trouble, because people would write me letters about what I had said. I said that the marketing system for beef was older than Christ. They were using a marketing system in those times, and it goes back at least to those days. I have used such terminology many times. I have said that the marketing system is older than Christ. Mr. Speaker, Christ threw the money changers out of the temple, because of the way they were trading. It was practically the same in beef. That means it is nearly 2,000 years old. I said it is as outdated as that marketing system.
The hon. member holds up the article. However, he does not point out all the good things. Anyone who knows me and knows how I live my life, knows that I am not kidding when I suggest that they pray for rain or pray for anything else. I may not appear to be a strong believer, but I am. These prayers have been answered. I see that when I look at the rainfall in the west. As late as yesterday morning the weather experts said they could see no rain.
Early in the year, in fact last fall, our people were concerned about moisture conditions as well as snow conditions in the mountains. We had continual reports on this throughout the year. We have done more than the United States. In the United States they might have been meeting with their governors. We will exchange this information with the United States Secretary of Agriculture and exchange aid and so on.
I will conclude by saying that if the hon. member would do a little more praying instead of making so much noise, it would do more good. We will be making a statement in the House tomorrow on our progress.
